title: The Rise of AI Software Clones: Why REA and ArtCraft Are Going Viral
abstract: The Rise of AI Software Clones: Why REA and ArtCraft Are Going Viral REA and ArtCraft are two projects driving a wave of AI-built clones that attempt to recreate Adobe and Microsoft software, letting developers reverse-engineer and rebuild commercial tools without access to the original source code. By Abid Ali Awan , KDnuggets Assistant Editor on October 12, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence Something crazy is happening in the AI development community, and I think we are witnessing the beginning of a major shift in the software industry. Developers are no longer just vibe coding websites, dashboards, and simple applications. They are attempting to recreate entire commercial software suites, including Adobe Creative Cloud and Microsoft Office. And the most interesting part? Some of these projects are being built by individual developers using AI coding agents. Two names in particular have caught my attention: Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) and ArtCraft . Why Are AI Software Clones Suddenly Going Viral? We already have free alternatives to commercial software. GIMP competes with Photoshop, Inkscape offers vector graphics editing, and LibreOffice provides alternatives to Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. But there has always been one major problem: switching costs. Most alternatives have their own interfaces, shortcuts, and workflows. If you have spent ten years mastering Photoshop, switching to GIMP can feel like learning an entirely different application. The new generation of AI-built clones is approaching this differently. Instead of reinventing the experience, developers are attempting to recreate familiar layouts, menus, shortcuts, and functionality. Imagine opening a free Photoshop alternative and immediately knowing where everything is. No extensive tutorials, no unfamiliar workflow, and potentially no expensive subscription. That is the promise, although the actual quality and compatibility of these early clones still vary considerably. REA Is Making Reverse Engineering More Accessible One of the most exciting projects behind this movement is Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) , an AI-powered reverse-engineering toolkit that has already attracted over 130,000 GitHub stars. Traditionally, reverse engineering required specialized knowledge, complicated tools, and hours of manual work. REA makes the process much easier by connecting AI coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor to tools such as Ghidra, Hopper, and IDA. The idea is simple: provide an application's binary, and your AI agent can analyze its functions, dependencies, architecture, and internal behavior without access to the original source code. You can then use those findings to recreate features or develop your own alternative. Developers are already experimenting with this approach. REA showcases include reconstructing Notion's clipboard functionality , recreating sound calculations from DX-Ball , and recovering mathematical routines from older PC-98 games. Imagine applying the same technique to expensive commercial software, rebuilding useful features, and sharing independently developed alternatives with the open-source community. REA cannot automatically produce a perfect clone, but it makes understanding existing software considerably easier. And I think that is what makes it so exciting. ArtCraft Is Already Recreating Adobe and Microsoft Software Developer Brandon Thomas has attracted attention for building a collection of Adobe-inspired applications using Claude and Rust. Image from PhotoCraft His projects include PhotoCraft for Photoshop-style image editing, VectorCraft for Illustrator-style graphics, and FilmCraft for Premiere-style video editing. The developer initially aimed for complete Adobe feature parity within a month — an ambitious target that has attracted plenty of skepticism. And the ambition does not stop with Adobe. The ArtCraft ecosystem now includes Microsoft Office-inspired projects: WordCraft recreates the familiar Microsoft Word ribbon and document-editing workflow. Its developer estimates approximately 62% real-world feature parity. GridCraft targets Excel, with support claimed for more than 500 spreadsheet functions. DeckCraft targets PowerPoint and reports 79% feature breadth but approximately 55% readiness as a practical replacement. Still, I find it fascinating that an individual developer can even attempt to build so many applications in such a short period. What Are People Saying About This? The reaction has been a mix of excitement and skepticism. Many developers are amazed that individuals can now recreate complex commercial software using AI agents, while creators are excited about having cheaper alternatives that look and feel like the tools they already use. However, others question whether these vibe-coded applications can match the reliability, performance, and functionality of mature software like Photoshop and Excel. Early testers have also raised concerns about bugs and missing features. Still, the overall excitement is hard to ignore. People are beginning to question why they should keep paying expensive subscriptions if AI-built alternatives can eventually deliver the same experience for free. My Final Thoughts What amazes me most is how quickly this is happening. REA only started gaining widespread attention around four days ago and has already attracted roughly 134,000 GitHub stars . That is incredible for a reverse-engineering tool. I can understand the excitement. Developers can now use AI to investigate expensive commercial software, recreate useful features, and share their alternatives with the open-source community. This could make sophisticated software more accessible to everyone. And this is not just about REA. Developers were already using AI coding agents to recreate popular applications long before it went viral. ArtCraft is just one example of a much bigger movement , where individuals and small teams are building software that previously required years of development. What excites me most is the potential shift in software ownership. Instead of relying on expensive subscriptions, people could run, customize, and own their software. Of course, these early clones still face challenges with reliability, compatibility, and intellectual property rights. I think the real threat to Adobe and Microsoft is not another free alternative. It is software that looks familiar, delivers the same essential features, and gives users no compelling reason to keep paying. And personally, I think we are just getting started. I am excited to see what developers build next. Abid Ali Awan ( @1abidaliawan ) is a certified data scientist professional who loves building machine learning models. Currently, he is focusing on content creation and writing technical blogs on machine learning and data science technologies. Abid holds a Master's degree in technology management and a bachelor's degree in telecommunication engineering. His vision is to build an AI product using a graph neural network for students struggling with mental illness. <= Previous post

title: ChatGPT vs. Claude vs. Gemini for Data Science Work: Here’s What I Found
abstract: ChatGPT vs. Claude vs. Gemini for Data Science Work: Here’s What I Found Compare ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini across the data science tasks that matter most to statisticians and analysts. By Vinod Chugani on October 12, 2026 in Data Science If you do any kind of data science work, you've probably tried at least one AI assistant. Maybe you asked it to explain a p-value, write a regression script, or help clean a messy dataset. ChatGPT , Claude , and Gemini are the three tools data scientists reach for most. I tested the current paid versions of all three on the same tasks: statistical test selection, conceptual explanations, Python code generation, exploratory data analysis, and longer document analysis. Here's what stood out. One caveat: all three platforms update their models frequently, so treat this as a snapshot rather than a permanent ranking. How Each Tool Approaches Data Science All three can generate Python and R code, explain statistical concepts, and walk you through analytical workflows. But the way they do it — and how reliably — varies quite a bit. ChatGPT operates as a broad generalist. Its biggest advantage for data science is its data analysis environment, which lets you upload CSV or Excel files, then writes and executes Python in a sandboxed environment within the conversation. You can go from raw data to summary statistics to a visualization without opening a notebook, and redirect mid-analysis ("remove those outliers and recalculate") on the fly. Claude tends to produce more detailed explanations and follows complex instructions closely across extended conversations. It now offers built-in code execution and file creation, so it can run Python on uploaded datasets and generate charts directly in the conversation. Give Claude a detailed prompt or a set of constraints and it sticks to them more consistently than the others. Gemini benefits from deep integration with Google's ecosystem. If your data lives in Google Sheets or Google Drive, Gemini can access it with minimal friction. It supports very large context windows and now includes built-in Python execution. For research tasks that require pulling together multiple sources, its web search gives it an edge. Statistical Reasoning and Explanation This is where the differences become most noticeable. When you ask a conceptual question — like explaining when to use a Welch's t-test instead of a standard independent samples t-test — all three give correct answers. The difference is in how they explain it. In my testing, Claude provided the most structured statistical reasoning, walking through assumptions, conditions, and implications in logical order without speculative jumps. A 2025 peer-reviewed study supports this pattern: researchers tested six AI assistants on 20 statistical test selection scenarios, and all achieved 100% accuracy. Claude received the highest rating for clarity, while Gemini scored highest for pedagogical value. Worth noting: the study tested free-tier versions on a single day, and several between-model differences were not statistically significant. ChatGPT gives solid problem-solving responses with practical context. It connects statistical concepts to scenarios you might encounter in business or research, which helps when you're trying to decide which test to apply to your own data. Gemini tends to frame explanations in ways that are easy to teach from or learn with. It also cross-references related concepts, helping you see how one technique connects to others. For straightforward questions, any of the three will serve you well. The gap shows up with multi-step reasoning — like choosing between modeling approaches for a dataset with specific properties. Claude and Gemini provide more methodical walkthroughs, while ChatGPT sometimes skips steps to reach the answer faster. Code Generation for Data Analysis All three now offer built-in code execution, so the distinction is less about which tool can run code and more about workflow and the quality of the resulting analysis. ChatGPT's data analysis environment is the most mature. You upload a dataset, describe what you want, and it writes Python, runs it, and returns results with visualizations. For exploratory data analysis (EDA), this workflow is very smooth. The limitation is that it works from uploaded files rather than live databases, and file sizes are restricted. In my testing, Claude produced the cleanest code for complex or multi-file tasks. If you need a data pipeline, a preprocessing class, or a refactored analysis script, Claude tends to generate better-organized output. Gemini handles code generation competently and works especially well when your code interacts with Google Cloud tools or BigQuery. One thing to note across all three: always verify generated code before running it on important data. All AI assistants can produce code with subtle statistical errors — like using wrong default parameters or misapplying a method's assumptions. Working with Large Datasets and Context Context window size matters when you're working with big datasets, long notebooks, or extensive documentation. The exact sizes depend on the model and plan, so check each platform's current documentation. Gemini generally offers the largest context windows. You can paste an entire notebook or technical report and ask questions about it, though output quality can vary at the extreme end. Claude supports large context windows and, in my experience, maintains reliability across long documents. For analyzing a lengthy report or working through a full codebase, it handles the task consistently. ChatGPT's context window is generally smaller but sufficient for most practical tasks. Where it compensates is with persistent memory, which retains your preferences across conversations. If you always work in Python with pandas, ChatGPT picks up those conventions automatically. Honest Limitations No AI assistant replaces a solid understanding of statistics. Each tool can produce output that sounds confident but contains methodological errors. All three can overlook assumptions that materially affect an analysis: independence, unequal variances, influential observations, model specification, or the distribution of residuals. They may recommend a statistically valid procedure without checking whether it fits the particular dataset and research question. In my experience, ChatGPT is more likely to push forward without flagging these issues, while Claude sometimes buries the core answer under so many caveats that it's hard to find. Gemini occasionally produces outdated library syntax or references deprecated functions, especially for less popular Python packages. Its explanations are generally accurate, but the code may need minor corrections before it runs cleanly. All three can hallucinate statistics — meaning they sometimes generate numbers, citations, or study results that don't actually exist. This matters most when you're relying on the tool for factual claims rather than code generation. Finally, consider data privacy. If you're working with proprietary or sensitive datasets, review each platform's data retention policies before uploading files. Web interfaces, API access, and enterprise tiers handle data differently, and the defaults may not meet your compliance requirements. Matching the Tool to Your Task The best choice depends on what you're actually doing. For exploratory data analysis on a single dataset , ChatGPT's data analysis environment is the most mature. You upload your file, ask questions, and get results with executed output. For understanding a statistical concept or choosing the right test , Claude tends to provide the most structured explanations. It walks through decision logic step by step. For research that requires current information or Google ecosystem integration , Gemini fits well. Its web search and Workspace connections save time when your work spans multiple tools.

title: 10 Hugging Face Models Worth Knowing in 2026
abstract: 10 Hugging Face Models Worth Knowing in 2026 Explore 10 Hugging Face models used across text, vision, audio, and retrieval in 2026. By Vinod Chugani on October 12, 2026 in Machine Learning The Hugging Face Hub reached nearly 3 million public model repositories in mid-2026, up from 2.43 million at the start of the year. For practitioners, the challenge is no longer access. It's knowing which models are worth your time, which have been superseded, and which are running in production pipelines regardless of what the benchmarks say. The ten models below were selected based on Hub adoption data, benchmark performance, licensing terms, and applicability to tasks that appear regularly in professional machine learning work. Several widely cited 2024 and 2025 models have been deliberately replaced by their successors. Where hardware or licensing requirements affect deployment, that's noted directly. All checkpoint names reference versions current at the time of publication. Verify the latest release on the Hugging Face Hub before running in production. All models in this article require recent library releases. Install or update the following before starting: pip install -U transformers diffusers sentence-transformers Code snippets appear where the interface is stable and the hardware is accessible on a standard developer machine. For larger or recently released models, a pointer to the model card quick-start is more honest than a snippet written against an API that may still be changing. Foundation and Reasoning Instruction-tuned models in this category share a loading pattern. Format your prompt using the chat template rather than passing a raw string: from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, AutoProcessor model_id = "your-chosen-checkpoint" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained( model_id, torch_dtype="auto", device_map="auto" ) Apply the chat template before tokenizing: messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Your prompt here"}] text = processor.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True) inputs = processor(text=text, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=200) print(processor.decode(outputs[0][inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True)) torch_dtype="auto" loads weights in the precision the model card specifies; device_map="auto" distributes layers across available GPUs. The decode line above slices off the input tokens before decoding, so you get just the model's response rather than the full prompt echoed back. The 27B model requires roughly 56 GB of VRAM at BF16, or around 16 GB with 4-bit quantization via bitsandbytes . For local experimentation, use google/gemma-4-E2B-it , which runs on a laptop or any consumer GPU; otherwise substitute Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B or any other Gemma 4 checkpoint. 1. Working with Qwen3.8-27B Qwen3.8-27B has become the default community base model in 2026. Qwen-derived repositories account for over 151,000 derivatives on the Hub, more than twice Meta's total footprint, and monthly GGUF downloads for the Qwen family exceed 39 million — more than five times the equivalent Llama figures. The 27B model is natively multimodal, processing images and video alongside text through a single checkpoint. That removes the need for separate vision-language weights, which simplifies both dependency management and deployment. The weights ship under the Apache 2.0 license. Qwen3-* checkpoints from 2025 are older models from the same family, so make sure the full version number is in the ID: use Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B to load the current model. 2. Reasoning at Scale with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is a multimodal mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 552 billion backbone parameters. It includes additional components that push the total weight size higher, but only activates 8 billion parameters per token during prefill and 16 billion during decode. It supports contexts up to one million tokens and is MIT licensed. At this scale, a Python loading snippet isn't a realistic entry point for most practitioners. The more direct path is through a serving framework: vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash --tensor-parallel-size 8 The --tensor-parallel-size 8 setting above is an example; check the model card for supported serving frameworks, weight conversion steps, and GPU requirements before running. The model is also available through Hugging Face Inference Providers, which lets you call it via the standard InferenceClient without managing the infrastructure. See the model card at huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash for the current quick-start. On coding tasks, it scores 74.2 on DeepSWE v1.1 and 90.6 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, among the strongest open-weight results on its model card's comparison table. One thing to watch: deepseek-chat and deepseek-reasoner were API model names, not Hub checkpoint IDs. Check the current DeepSeek API documentation for updated endpoint names if you were calling those through an API client. 3. Deploying at the Edge with Gemma 4 Gemma 4 , released by Google in April 2026, covers the on-device and edge deployment use case. The family launched in four sizes, from the E2B ( google/gemma-4-E2B-it ) designed for smartphones and laptops up to the 31B Dense variant ( google/gemma-4-31B-it ). All four ship under the Apache 2.0 license, a meaningful change from the source-available terms that governed earlier Gemma releases. Use the shared chat-template pattern from the Foundation and Reasoning section with whichever checkpoint fits your hardware. The E2B variant is the recommended starting point for local experimentation. The 31B Dense variant ranked third on the Arena AI text leaderboard at launch, but the smaller checkpoints are what make this family relevant for constrained deployment environments. Retrieval and Representation 4. Classifying Text with ModernBERT-base Not every task needs a generative decoder. For fine-tuned text classification, named entity recognition (NER), and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) indexing, an encoder-only model is the more efficient tool. ModernBERT-base extends the original BERT context window to 8,192 tokens and adds Flash Attention for faster inference at longer sequence lengths. The right use case for ModernBERT is fine-tuning on labeled data, not zero-shot prompting. A minimal training loop: from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification, Trainer, TrainingArguments model_id = "answerdotai/ModernBERT-base" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(model_id, num_labels=4) Pass your tokenized datasets objects to the Trainer: args = TrainingArguments(output_dir="modernbert-classifier", num_train_epochs=3, per_device_train_batch_size=16, eval_strategy="epoch") trainer = Trainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=train_ds, eval_dataset=eval_ds) trainer.train() After fine-tuning on domain-specific data, ModernBERT typically outperforms zero-shot alternatives, and inference stays fast enough for production throughput on standard GPU hardware. 5. Building Retrieval Pipelines with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B currently leads the open-weight Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) leaderboard at its parameter count, with 596 million parameters and a default output dimension of 1,024. Output dimensions are flexible, supporting user-defined sizes from 32 to 1,024, which matters when storage or retrieval latency is a constraint. This model uses last-token pooling with L2 normalization, not mean pooling. It also expects an instruction prefix for query inputs. The sentence-transformers integration handles both: from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer model = SentenceTransformer("Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B") query = model.encode("What is retrieval-augmented generation?

title: AI models may be capable of self-replicating without access to a datacenter
abstract: Frontier Red Team AI models may be capable of self-replicating without access to a datacenter Oct 12, 2026 William Zhou, Daniel Freeman Our experiments suggest that small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial IoT devices, like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes. A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off - though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own. In our evals, a 9B model got inference running on 8 of the 9 hardware types we tested. Models of 30B parameters and under can already complete many of the individual steps for replication today, though they make mistakes when composing them end to end. In our simplified evals, GLM-5.2 and stronger models are capable of end to end replication. If small models improve at their historical rate, they’ll match this capability level by the end of this year. Small weight-based replicators may be possible soon after. Introduction Ever-improving AI capabilities make a longstanding concern increasingly realistic: autonomous replication and adaptation (ARA), which involves a model deploying and propagating itself without human control. In cyber, a worm is a program that copies itself from one computer to the next without human input. Prior work has already shown that AI agents can act like one: scanning their network, executing an exploit, and copying model weights to a target machine across a GPU cluster. Such an “AI worm” could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware. Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload. Datacenter GPUs would be a clear, high-value target for such malware. But expensive accelerators aren’t strictly necessary. In this blog post, we show that a distributed botnet of IoT devices—which are cheap and typically poorly defended—could also provide enough compute to run a capable model. We run Gemma4-26B-A4B, distributed over 15 inexpensive off-brand Android TV boxes (~$55 each) that we bought and networked together, at 0.39 tokens per second. Each tile below shows one physical TV box holding two of the model’s layers as the model runs. A fleet of 15 Smart TV boxes running distributed inference of Gemma4-26B-A4B. Of course, there are many other steps to showing that an autonomous worm can propagate itself across a network of weak machines. For the purposes of this blog post, we break down the replication chain into a few steps. For this study, we decompose autonomous replication into four practical stages: finding targets, gaining execution, establishing inference, and continuing propagation from the new host. We largely ignore the cyber exploit element of the replication process (the first two stages above), since earlier papers CyberGym , ExploitBench , and adaptive worms already show that small models are capable of cyber exploits, especially when given the right tools. But a less commonly measured part of the replication process involves setting up inference on compromised devices, which is our focus here. In this post, we first lay out the threat models that we think are most likely to be realized. Then, we test whether small models can set up inference on unfamiliar hardware, and whether they can chain the full replication cycle together across a fleet of machines. After that, we estimate how fast such a worm could spread, and test whether it could learn and adapt as it replicates. We conclude with how AI worms would differ from pre-AI malware, and brief suggestions for defenses against such replicators. Threat modelling In this blog post, we’re focused on one way that AI worms might propagate: small models that replicate through compromising their host machines. But there are several other methods that AI worms might try: they could steal access in order to spin up hosts (for example, API keys or platform credentials) or pay for inference through legitimate work (e.g digital freelancing). The threat models that we think are closest to being realized today are the following: A small model, replicating via host compromise. In this post, we’ll call autonomous worms that run their models directly on compromised hardware weight-based replicators . Home and small business IoT devices might be the first target for such attacks because they’re connected to the internet and, historically, have had minimal security measures in place. A model that’s too large to fit on one device can be split into pieces, or shards, that run on separate machines that communicate with each other to collectively run the model. Machines that could run a significant model shard for a <30B model include smart fridges, smart ovens, automatic vacuum cleaners, and lawnmowers. A growing number of home and business devices, such as security cameras and video-conferencing units now ship with small built-in AI chips, designed to run AI models on the device itself. This extra computing power will likely make them attractive targets as well. Human hackers often breach secure systems through social engineering (for example, convincing a company’s IT department that you’re an employee who forgot your password) rather than hacking. This tradeoff appears to be flipped for today’s small models, which are relatively strong at agentic coding and hacking compared to their social engineering capabilities (see Appendix E), though this might change as models improve. A large, advanced weight-based replicator focused on datacenters and other high-compute targets. Larger models tend to have correspondingly better cyber capabilities, but will also need to breach (relatively) hardened datacenters to run themselves. We split this threat model into two subcategories: Frontier replicators: Large closed-weight replicators run on their lab’s infrastructure, and can spin up unmonitored internal deployments or exfiltrate their weights onto external compute. Open-weight replicators: These replicators start off relatively lower-resourced (due to not benefitting from a lab’s compute), but start unmonitored. An API-based replicator, in which a model would replicate by stealing credentials for their own inference API. These replicators would require a model provider to unknowingly serve them, and their persistence may be worse, since they’d likely be easier to discover (although their rate of spread may be higher, if for instance they’re able to replicate using victims’ accounts). In practice, an AI worm wouldn’t necessarily consist of just one model or strategy. A swarm of different models deployed on different types of hardware using a variety of replication schemes might represent a more realistic ‘worst case scenario’ attack. In this blog post, we consider the feasibility of small weight-based replicators (section 1 of the above). We focus on this because it’s a near-term threat model that can be investigated directly. Our demo at the top of this post, a 26B model running across 15 boxes, shows that IoT devices can run surprisingly capable models. Could these models be capable enough to carry out autonomous replication? We examine this in two parts. First, can small models get a model running on unfamiliar hardware? And second, can they do the whole cycle (find an uninfected device, copy themselves over, start running there, and repeat) all together in a single run? A. Inference setup Of the stages in the above diagram showing the replication cycle, inference setup is the least studied and may be the most challenging for small models. It requires a fairly long sequence of hardware and OS-specific decisions around picking a compatible inference stack, finding the right versions of packages, and debugging machine-specific issues. These steps are serially dependent, and failures are difficult to recover from.

title: Large Language Models for Machine Translation Quality Annotation: Humans and Models Are Both Challenged
abstract: research area Speech and Natural Language Processing conference EMNLP content type paper published October 2026 Large Language Models for Machine Translation Quality Annotation: Humans and Models Are Both Challenged Authors Hala Almaghout, Christian Federmann, Qin Gao View publication Copy Bibtex Large Language Models (LLMs) are considered to be a more efficient and cost-effective alternative to human judgment for Machine Translation (MT) evaluation. With MT evaluation spanning a large number of language pairs, domains and levels of annotation granularity, LLMs must be thoroughly evaluated across these dimensions before being reliably used as alternatives to human evaluation. In this paper, we evaluate the performance of LLMs for two prominent MT quality evaluation schemes: Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM) and Error Span Annotation (ESA) by comparing their agreement with human annotators. We present results on a long-context test set of 70 language pairs and the publicly available WMT23 and WMT25 data, investigating both score and error span annotation agreement across a variety of language pairs and domains. Our results show that while LLM agreement with human annotators exceeds agreement between human annotators for some evaluation tasks, both vary substantially across annotation schemes, language pairs and domains and remain unreliable for most settings. Furthermore, we identify challenges facing both human and LLM annotators: humans are particularly challenged by fine-grained MQM annotations and low-resource language pairs, while LLMs struggle with minor errors, wrong language variants and error span annotation. Our results highlight the potential for improvement for both human and LLM annotation performance, possibly through human-LLM collaborative annotation pipelines that address the reliability issues identified in this work. title: Minions: A Dynamic and Distributed Virtual GPU Cloud Built on Idle Apple Silicon Devices
abstract: research area Speech and Natural Language Processing , research area Tools, Platforms, Frameworks content type paper published October 2026 Minions: A Dynamic and Distributed Virtual GPU Cloud Built on Idle Apple Silicon Devices Authors Jianhua Li, Yun Xing, Girisha De Silva, Ryan Flint, Kai Yuan, Sean Suchter View publication Copy Bibtex The increasing demand for GPU-accelerated machine learning inference has exposed limitations in centralized GPU infrastructures, including high cost, limited elasticity, and long wait times under resource constraints. At the same time, modern Apple Silicon–based macOS devices are equipped with powerful GPUs that remain largely idle during normal usage. This paper presents Minions, a dynamic and distributed virtual GPU cloud that aggregates idle Apple Silicon GPUs across macOS devices to execute large-scale machine learning inference workloads. Minions enables teams to leverage existing hardware without requiring additional GPU procurement. The system provides flexible GPU inference task execution, fault tolerance, and efficient resource utilization. Our experience shows that idle macOS devices can be transformed into a practical distributed GPU inference platform in environments where centralized GPU resources are constrained. title: Self-Compacting Language Model Agents
abstract: research area Speech and Natural Language Processing conference NeurIPS content type paper published October 2026 Self-Compacting Language Model Agents Authors Tianjian Li†, Jingyu Zhang†, William Jurayj†, Xi Wang†, Chuanyang Jin†, Mehrdad Farajtabar, Eric Nalisnick†, Daniel Khashabi† View publication Copy Bibtex Long agent traces composed of chains of thought and tool calls accumulate stale content that anchor subsequent generations, and eventually outgrow the context window. Existing scaffolds mitigate it with fixed-interval compaction triggered at a token threshold. Such triggers pay no heed to trajectory structure, risking discard of partial results mid-derivation or mid-search. We propose SELFCOMPACT, a scaffold that allows the model itself to decide when and how to compact. Specifically, it pairs two inference-time elements: (i) a compaction tool the model invokes to summarize the accumulated context, and (ii) a lightweight rubric specifying when to fire (a sub-task has resolved, or the trajectory is converging) and when to suppress (mid-derivation, or when stuck). Both are needed. The tool alone is unevenly used across open-weight models, often invoked at unhelpful moments or not at all; the rubric alone cannot act. Together, they elicit effective adaptive compaction without any fine-tuning or external supervision. We present empirical results on six benchmarks (competitive math and agentic search) and seven models. Our results show that SELFCOMPACT matches or exceeds fixed-interval summarization at a fraction of the token cost, improving over a no-summarization baseline by up to 18.1 points on math and 5–9 points on agentic search at 30–70% lower per-question cost. Our results expose a meta-cognitive gap: although unprompted models cannot reliably tell when their own context is rotting, a lightweight rubric closes this gap, reframing when to compact as a capability that scaffolds can supply without training. † Johns Hopkins University Related readings and updates.
