title: ReplaySSM: Rethinking State Storage for Faster Hybrid-Model Decoding
abstract: Hybrid models interleave state-space model (SSM) layers with a few attention layers. NVIDIA Nemotron 3 , Qwen3.5 through Qwen3.8 , Kimi-K3 , and GLM-5.3-Flash are all built this way, with Mamba-2 , Gated DeltaNet (GDN) , or Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) as the SSM layer. SSM layers are designed to make decoding fast: they use a fixed-size state in place of a key-value (KV) cache that grows with context length. At serving batch sizes, however, the SSM layers, not attention, can be the latency bottleneck up to 100K tokens of context. SSM layers also complicate two techniques that reliably speed up attention decoding: speculative decoding and quantization. ReplaySSM makes SSM layers the fast part again. It represents the SSM state as a checkpoint plus a buffer of recent inputs. This separates output computation from state updates and addresses three challenges in current SSM decoding: state traffic, rollback for speculative decoding, and error accumulation in a quantized state. ReplaySSM is joint work between NVIDIA and the Dao AI Lab at Princeton. The paper, ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State , details all three benefits and presents the full evaluation. It is available on arXiv, with code on GitHub . It is integrated into NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, and FlashInfer, and also runs in production in GLM-5.3-Flash and Kimi-K3. Figure 1. Conventional decoding loads and stores the full state at every step. ReplaySSM caches recent inputs, computes outputs from the checkpoint plus buffer, and writes the checkpoint only when the buffer fills Why SSM layers can become a decoding bottleneck Take the Mamba-2 layer used in NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra as an example. It decodes one token with the following recurrence: S t = α t S t − 1 + v t k t ⊤ , o t = S t q t , S_t = \alpha_t S_{t-1} + v_t k_t^\top, \qquad o_t = S_t q_t, where S t S_t is the state, α t \alpha_t is a data-dependent decay, and v t v_t , k t k_t , and q t q_t are the token’s inputs. Each step loads S t − 1 S_{t-1} from high-bandwidth memory (HBM), applies the decay and a rank-1 update, computes the output with q t q_t , and stores S t S_t back. GDN and KDA add a delta-rule correction, but their updates can be written in the same outer-product form, so what follows applies to them too. During decoding, the state does two jobs. It is read to produce this token’s output, and it is updated to become the next token’s state. Conventional decoding does both at once: each step updates the state, reads the output from it, and stores it for the next step. All three challenges come from this fusion. Figure 2. Three challenges of conventional SSM decoding and the ReplaySSM answer to each. Left: decode-step latency breakdown for Nemotron-3-Super-NVFP4 at batch size 256 on one NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra B300 GPU State memory traffic An SSM decoding step loads and stores the full state while performing little arithmetic on it, so the kernel is bound by HBM bandwidth, not compute. At serving batch sizes, that makes the SSM layers, not attention, the largest component of the decode step up to 100K tokens on Nemotron-3-Super-NVFP4 at batch size 256 on one NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra B300 GPU (Figure 2, left). Two factors drive this: Layer count: The model has five times as many SSM layers as attention layers. State size: One layer’s FP32 state is 4 MiB per sequence, while an FP8 KV entry is 0.5 KiB per token, so an SSM layer’s state is the size of an attention layer’s KV cache for 8K tokens. Rollback for speculative decoding Speculative decoding has a drafter propose T tokens, verifies them in one pass through the target model, and rolls back to the last accepted token. Attention naturally supports rollback by moving the KV cache pointer. But once an SSM has summarized the drafts into its state, the update has no easy inverse, so rollback becomes expensive. Serving engines such as vLLM work around this by storing a state snapshot after every draft token and picking the one that matches the accepted prefix. That is one read and T writes per step on a memory-bound path, and the snapshots cap how many requests fit in GPU memory. As a result, speculative decoding, a reliable speedup for Transformers, barely helps SSMs at serving batch sizes. State quantization The quantized state produces the output and is the input to the next update, so its rounding error re-enters the recurrence at every step. A KV cache has no such loop: a quantized entry is read many times but never written back into itself, which is why KV caches tolerate lower precision than SSM states. Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-NVFP4, for example, uses the NVIDIA NVFP4 4-bit floating-point format for its weights, with an FP8 KV cache and an FP32 SSM state. How ReplaySSM represents the state The SSM recurrence can be unrolled over a window of h tokens: S t = α t S t − 1 + v t k t ⊤ = γ h S c k p t + ∑ j = 1 h γ j + 1 : h v j k j ⊤ , S_t = \alpha_t S_{t-1} + v_t k_t^\top = \gamma_h\, S_{\mathrm{ckpt}} + \sum_{j=1}^{h} \gamma_{j+1:h}\, v_j k_j^\top, where S c k p t S_{\mathrm{ckpt}} is the state before the window and γ \gamma is the cumulative decay. Conventional decoding follows the left side step by step. ReplaySSM uses the right side: it represents the state as a checkpoint plus a small buffer of recent input records ( α j \alpha_j , v j v_j , k j k_j ) for Mamba-2. On most steps, which we call non-flush steps, it appends the current inputs to the buffer and computes the output from the checkpoint and the buffer without storing a state. When the buffer of L records fills, a flush step folds the buffered inputs into the checkpoint, writes the new checkpoint to HBM once, and clears the buffer. The outputs match conventional decoding up to floating-point differences. ReplaySSM’s approach can be summarized in three questions: 1 What does ReplaySSM do? It caches recent SSM inputs and represents the state as a checkpoint plus those inputs. 2 What does this change? It separates output computation from state updates: outputs are computed every step, while the checkpoint is updated once per window. 3 What does this achieve? It reduces state memory traffic, simplifies speculative rollback, and supports low-precision state reads without propagating their rounding error through recurrent updates. How we evaluated ReplaySSM We evaluate four hybrid models from two families, Nemotron 3 with Mamba-2 layers and Qwen3.5 with GDN layers, from 4B dense models on one NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU to 120B-class mixture-of-experts (MoE) models on one NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra B300 GPU (Table 1). We implemented ReplaySSM in vLLM and compared it with vLLM’s own kernels at their best launch configuration. Performance runs keep the SSM state in FP32, the default precision for these models, and use a window of L = 16, the best-performing window size for all four models. Speculative decoding tests use each model’s multi-token prediction (MTP) head to generate draft tokens. Model SSM layer Weights GPU SSM / attention layers Nemotron-3-Nano-4B Mamba-2 BF16 1×H100 21 / 4 Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B Mamba-2 NVFP4 1×B300 40 / 8 Qwen3.5-4B GDN BF16 1×H100 24 / 8 Qwen3.5-122B-A10B GDN NVFP4 1×B300 36 / 12 Table 1. Evaluated models and hardware. Each model runs on one GPU without tensor parallelism Benefit 1: Reduce state memory traffic Over a window of L tokens, conventional decoding reads the state L times and writes it L times. ReplaySSM still reads the checkpoint on every step, because the output needs it, but writes it only once, during the flush. A non-flush step has one job—computing the output—and writes only the new input record, a few vectors instead of a full matrix. This roughly halves the dominant state traffic. At serving batch sizes, memory bandwidth limits the conventional kernel’s performance, so reducing state memory traffic speeds up decoding. At batch size 1, other sources of latency dominate, and ReplaySSM provides no speedup in these tests. At batch size 256, the kernel runs 1.46× to 1.

title: Accessing OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock with global cross-Region inference in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Taiwan
abstract: Single-Region inference can throttle when demand exceeds local capacity. Teams in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Taiwan need access to the newest OpenAI models beyond that capacity. Amazon Bedrock offers OpenAI GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna through global cross-Region inference from all five AWS Regions, and GPT-6 Astra from Asia Pacific (Singapore). This post shows you how to configure the call, set permissions, and monitor inference from your source Region. GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6 Astra are all available through global cross-Region inference from the preceding Regions, on the bedrock-runtime endpoint. See Cross-Region inference in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. For the full list of source and destination Regions in each profile, see Supported Regions and models for inference profiles . In this post, we introduce the global cross-Region inference profiles and invoke them from Asia Pacific (Singapore) using the Converse API, the OpenAI-compatible APIs, and coding clients. We then cover the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and service control policy (SCP) configuration, quota management, and monitoring. The GPT-6 family offers three models, each available through global cross-Region inference. All three accept text and image input, client-side tool use, and prompt caching. They differ on reasoning effort. GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna accept none, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. GPT-6 Astra accepts the same levels except none. For GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, see Bring more intelligence to everyday work with GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna on Amazon Bedrock . For GPT-6 Astra, see Take on your most ambitious work with GPT-6 Astra on Amazon Bedrock . Global cross-Region inference routes requests across supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed, giving you broad access to Amazon Bedrock capacity. You invoke it by passing a global cross-Region inference profile ID in place of a model ID. Your source Region is where you make the API call. Amazon Bedrock selects the destination Region for processing. Billing, quota tracking, AWS CloudTrail, and Amazon CloudWatch all stay in your source Region. The following table lists the global cross-Region inference profile IDs and the source Regions covered in this post. Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1 Asia Pacific (Jakarta) ap-southeast-3 Asia Pacific (Malaysia) ap-southeast-5 Asia Pacific (Thailand) ap-southeast-7 Asia Pacific (Taipei) ap-east-2 Inference profile availability and Region support change as AWS adds Regions and profiles, so confirm both on the model card before you build: GPT-6 Sol , GPT-6 Luna , and GPT-6 Astra . For per-token rates, see Amazon Bedrock pricing . Start with the prerequisites, then invoke any of the three profiles through the Converse API, the OpenAI-compatible APIs, or your existing coding client. The Amazon Bedrock console lists all three global cross-Region inference profiles under system-defined inference profiles. See Figure 1. Figure 1: The three global OpenAI GPT-6 inference profiles among the system-defined profiles in the Amazon Bedrock console Each model supports three access paths on this endpoint: the Amazon Bedrock Converse API, the OpenAI Responses API, and the OpenAI Chat Completions API. The OpenAI-compatible APIs are called on the /openai/v1 paths rather than through the AWS SDKs, and the endpoint accepts either Signature Version 4 (SigV4) or an Amazon Bedrock API key. Pass the global cross-Region inference profile ID as the model in every case. Converse API. This example calls GPT-6 Sol from Asia Pacific (Singapore) and logs the response. Set BEDROCK_PROFILE_ID to global.openai.gpt-6-luna or global.openai.gpt-6-astra to switch models, or call converse_stream for streaming. OpenAI Chat Completions API. Point the OpenAI SDK at the Regional endpoint and pass the same profile ID. When migrating an existing OpenAI client: The ChatGPT desktop app and the Codex CLI share ~/.codex/config.toml , so one change covers both. Of the two built-in Amazon Bedrock providers, only amazon-bedrock-runtime accepts an inference profile. SigV4 signing means there is no key to rotate. Add profile = "<your-profile>" for a non-default profile, and set region explicitly, because the client otherwise falls back to AWS_REGION . Substitute another profile ID for model to change models. Codex reports a 272,000-token window for these profiles, which is its own bundled figure rather than a service limit. Raise it with model_context_window . This configuration needs Codex CLI 0.148 or later. Figure 2 shows the result in the app. Figure 2: The ChatGPT desktop app running GPT-6 Astra on Amazon Bedrock Amazon Bedrock offers a range of controls over inference. Two of them matter here. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies control which roles can invoke which profiles, and service control policies (SCPs) apply organization-wide controls, including Region scope. This section covers both, and where request data lands. To call any of these models through a global cross-Region inference profile, your IAM policy needs four statements: This IAM policy grants permission to invoke GPT-6 Sol through global cross-Region inference from ap-southeast-1 . Replace with your AWS account ID and ap-southeast-1 with your source Region. If you use streaming ( converse_stream or stream=True ), add bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream to the Action in the first three statements. Converse authorizes as bedrock:InvokeModel . If you only call Converse with SigV4 credentials, drop the fourth statement. To switch models, replace openai.gpt-6-sol with openai.gpt-6-luna or openai.gpt-6-astra throughout. For the complete reference, see IAM policy requirements for global cross-Region inference . A global cross-Region inference request carries no Region name. Amazon Bedrock sets aws:RequestedRegion to unspecified , so a Region allowlist in an SCP denies the call, and the error names only the policy type, not which policy. That is a common reason a first call fails in an enterprise account. Rather than widening the allowlist, scope the exception. Amazon Bedrock populates the bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition key during authorization, so an SCP can allow these profiles while keeping Region controls for everything else. The following SCP does that. The first statement enforces your Region allowlist for every service except Amazon Bedrock inference. The second denies that inference outside those Regions unless it routes through a global cross-Region inference profile. For geographic profiles, add their prefix (for example inference-profile/us.* ) to the ArnNotLike list, because geographic requests carry a real Region name. Keep your source Region in the allowlist, and add the global services your organization uses to NotAction . A blunter alternative is to add unspecified to your existing allowlist, which works but opens the same exception to every other service. For a ready-to-use policy file, see the aws-samples service-control-policy-examples repository . For automated offline abuse detection, classifier-flagged traffic is retained by AWS for up to 30 days and processed programmatically. Under cross-Region inference that retention happens in the destination Region, which for a global profile is any supported commercial AWS Region where the model is deployed. Eligible customers might request full zero data retention through their AWS account team. For more information, see Amazon Bedrock abuse detection and Data retention . If your organization has data residency requirements, take this to your risk and compliance team early. See the AWS Financial Services Compliance Center country pages for these five countries. We recommend you obtain your own advice on compliance with the requirements relevant to your business. GPT-6 quotas on bedrock-runtime are measured in tokens per minute (TPM), tracked against the source Region you call from.

title: Deploy decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI
abstract: Applications that route requests, select agent actions, or assign policy outcomes often need scores over a fixed set of choices instead of free-form text. Deploying these decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI gives you a managed path for serving quantized models on CPU or GPU infrastructure. This post continues a series on specialized AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) for generative AI inference. Previous posts cover WhisperX , vLLM-Omni – Part 1 , and vLLM-Omni – Part 2 . In this post, you first use the AWS DLC for llama.cpp to serve OpenAI-compatible chat completions through SageMaker AI InvokeEndpoint . You then extend the same runtime with SemIf , formerly OpenJev, which returns probabilities over declared options without decoding an answer token. The accompanying code sample includes CPU and GPU deployment options. Figure 1 shows two deployment paths from the same packaged model. The text-generation path uses the AWS DLC for llama.cpp and returns generated responses through the OpenAI-compatible API. The structured-decision path builds a child image that replaces the default server with a SemIf adapter and returns probabilities for declared options. Figure 1: Run the AWS DLC for llama.cpp or the SemIf child image on CPU or GPU, depending on the API and latency requirements of your workload For the standard path, package the model as model.tar.gz in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and reference the published DLC image directly. The container finds the first .gguf file under /opt/ml/model , maps POST /invocations to llama-server at /v1/chat/completions , and passes SM_LLAMA_CPP_* environment variables to llama.cpp arguments. The llama-server HTTP API doesn’t expose the final-position logits and state operations that SemIf uses. The structured-decision path therefore uses AWS CodeBuild to build a child image and store it in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) . The child image keeps the DLC’s compiled CPU or CUDA libraries while replacing its entry point with a SageMaker-compatible adapter. The AWS DLC for llama.cpp accepts the OpenAI Chat Completions schema. Send a messages array with role and content , plus generation controls such as max_tokens and stream : The response uses the OpenAI-compatible choices array. Read generated text from choices[0].message.content . SemIf uses a constrained decision schema instead of chat messages. The request contains a caller-defined ID, unstructured state, a question, and an ordered list of allowed options: The response returns option_ids , probabilities , and raw option_logits in the same order, along with prompt, timing, and pinned model metadata. With stable option IDs, your application can apply thresholds, fallbacks, and policy checks without parsing generated prose. SemIf belongs to a broader class of decision models that score application-defined outcomes from unstructured state. Other implementations include Jev , TypeSafe’s decision model and /v1/systemone API; Kev , a model server designed for TypeSafe API compatibility; and Strands Decider 2B , a purpose-built model for agent workflows with calibrated outputs. Use this pattern when your application defines the allowed choices at request time and needs a model to interpret unstructured context. Examples include routing a case to a queue, extracting one value from a known set, assigning an incident priority, checking a policy outcome, or selecting an agent action. Keep authorization and deterministic business rules outside the model, and validate model probabilities before treating them as operational confidence. Use the standard SageMaker AI text-generation path when you need OpenAI-compatible chat completions through InvokeEndpoint . The SageMaker AI image maps POST /invocations to the llama-server /v1/chat/completions endpoint. Build a child image only when your application needs behavior that this interface doesn’t provide, such as SemIf’s direct logits and state access. Removing answer-token generation doesn’t remove model inference. The model still processes the complete state, question, and option descriptions before SemIf reads the final logits. Keep prompts focused, and evaluate the selected model with labeled decisions from your application before production use. The following benchmark applies to the SemIf extension, not the text-generation endpoint. Model size, quantization, prompt length, runtime, and CPU thread count affect each decision. To quantify these trade-offs, we sent the same 231 public JevBench tasks serially to one CPU endpoint and one GPU endpoint. Compared with the CPU configuration, the GPU endpoint was 4.9 times faster at p50 and 32.2 times faster at p95. The sample uses the SageMaker AI instance pools feature to list compatible GPU instance types in priority order, so SageMaker can select an alternative when the first preference isn’t available. The pool ordered g6e , g6 , g5 , then g4dn . SageMaker selected ml.g6e.xlarge , and startup logs confirmed that llama.cpp offloaded all 34 model layers to an NVIDIA L40S. The CPU and GPU images used different llama.cpp builds and produced different predictions on six hard tasks. Treat the one-answer accuracy difference as runtime variation, not evidence that GPU offload improves model quality. Smaller models reduced median latency, but the 2B and 0.8B candidates achieved 66.7 percent and 58.4 percent accuracy. The sample therefore keeps the 4B Q4_K_M model as its quality-first default. These measurements include network latency and aren’t service guarantees. Benchmark the complete model and infrastructure configuration against your own decisions. Use CPU for background, offline, or low-throughput workloads that aren’t latency-sensitive and can tolerate seconds of response time. Use GPU for interactive decisions, long prompts, or workloads with tight tail-latency targets. Keep state and option descriptions concise, group decisions that share the same state into one request, and scale endpoint instances for concurrency. Shared-state scoring reuses the common prompt prefix, while the adapter returns retryable HTTP 503 responses instead of allowing an unbounded queue around its stateful llama.cpp context. The text-generation example uses the CPU DLC and a fixed CPU instance. The SemIf extension keeps CPU as the default for workloads that aren’t latency-sensitive and offers an optional CUDA image with ordered instance pools. Review SageMaker AI pricing before creating an endpoint. Use the following procedure to deploy the standard text-generation endpoint, then build the optional SemIf extension for structured decisions on CPU or GPU. Wait for the returned build ID to reach SUCCEEDED . The build records the source revisions and checksums in model-manifest.json and stops if the GGUF checksum differs from the validated value. Resolve a digest-pinned server-sagemaker-cpu-v1 image from the AWS DLC for llama.cpp documentation , then create the SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint: Select a server-sagemaker-cpu-v1 or server-sagemaker-cuda-v1 image rather than the corresponding EC2 image. The SageMaker AI images implement the /ping and /invocations container contract and map invocation payloads to chat completions. This walkthrough supplies the GGUF model through the SageMaker AI model artifact in Amazon S3. As an alternative, you can configure SM_LLAMA_CPP_HF_REPO and SM_LLAMA_CPP_HF_FILE to download a GGUF file from Hugging Face when the endpoint has network egress. You don’t need a Dockerfile or an ECR repository for this path. Wait for the endpoint to enter InService , then send an OpenAI-compatible chat request: For GPU, build the CUDA child image instead: After the build succeeds, construct the immutable image URI: The deployment script rejects mutable image tags. The CPU configuration uses a fixed instance type: Wait for the returned endpoint name to enter InService . This path sets n_gpu_layers=0 .

title: Run multi-node inference workloads using Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers
abstract: This post shows how to deploy one large language model (LLM) across two GPU nodes on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with the multi-node Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers . It uses separate prefill and decode nodes behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. This kind of multi-node setup is common for tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism, as well as prefill/decode disaggregation inference workloads. In a previous post , we introduced the Ray Serve DLC and used it to stand up a small model behind an HTTP endpoint on a single GPU node. You had a working inference endpoint, and the container keeps the GPU stack compatible, including CUDA libraries, so you did not need to write boilerplate code. Ray is a distributed compute framework, so Ray Serve deployments can span multiple nodes. Customers use multi-node Ray Serve for several reasons. Some want to run foundation or open-weight models that are too large for a single GPU. Others need more throughput than one replica can deliver. Still others want to separate the two phases of inference to improve performance. In each case, customers must build the dependency chain themselves: choosing compatible libraries for the GPU stack and debugging issues when a component drifts out of alignment. This is undifferentiated work that takes time and effort away from delivering models. AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) have long solved this kind of problem for training and inferencing workloads. DLCs are pre-built, performance-optimized Docker images that bundle a framework, its dependencies, and the GPU stack into a tested, patched combination you can pull and use immediately. With the launch of the Ray LLM DLC for multi-node deployments, that same approach now extends to multi-node inference. You get a container purpose-built for serving models behind an HTTP endpoint, maintained and tested by AWS, with the full inference stack already assembled. This post walks through implementing multi-node disaggregated inference using multi-node Ray LLM DLC: deploying a single large language model across two GPU-powered nodes on Amazon EKS cooperating behind a single endpoint. While one of the GPU nodes handles the prefill phase, the other GPU node handles the decode phase. Separating the phases prevents compute-heavy long prompts from stalling token generation for requests already in progress. This approach is well suited for workloads such as Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), document summarization, and agentic applications. We use the multi-node Ray LLM DLC, which ships Ray Serve LLM , NVIDIA Inference Transfer Library (NIXL) , and the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) stack, and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with no application code. The complete code is available in the accompanying repository . LLM inference has two distinct phases. Prefill processes the entire input prompt in parallel and builds the key-value (KV) cache. Decode then generates the response one token at a time, reading and extending that cache. Prefill is compute bound, and Decode is bound by memory bandwidth. When both phases share one GPU, they contend for the same resources, and the bursty, compute-heavy prefill work interferes with the steady, latency-sensitive decode work. Separating the prefill phase from the decode phase means you can select the hardware and serving properties for each phase, improving overall performance at scale. PD disaggregation places the two phases on separate nodes, so each phase runs without interfering with the other and can be scaled independently. The trade-off is that the KV cache built during prefill must be handed to the decode node, and that transfer should be fast enough not to erase the benefit. That is exactly why the interconnect between the nodes matters. AWS DLCs are pre-built, performance-optimized Docker images that bundle a framework, its dependencies, and the GPU stack into a tested, patched combination you can pull and use immediately. All components are validated together before each release, so there is no version drift between the CUDA runtime, the framework, and the serving layer. Security patches are applied at build time. The Ray LLM DLC extends this to distributed LLM serving. It ships vLLM as the inference engine, Ray Serve’s HTTP as the serving layer, NIXL for KV-cache transfer between nodes, and the EFA stack ( libfabric and aws-ofi-nccl ) for high-bandwidth node-to-node communication. Because the Ray Serve LLM library includes a built-in application builder, the entire serving application is a block of YAML. There’s no handler class, no model archiver, and no custom image to build. A single helper, build_pd_openai_app , takes a prefill configuration and a decode configuration and wires the KV-cache transfer between them behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The following diagram shows how the deployment is laid out on Amazon EKS. A user request reaches the Ray head on the CPU system node, and the two GPU worker nodes run the prefill and decode phases of the model. Figure 1: Multi-node inference architecture on Amazon EKS, with the Ray head on a CPU system node and the prefill and decode phases on two GPU worker nodes The deployment is an EKS cluster inside a virtual private cloud (VPC). Nodes run in private subnets with outbound access through a NAT Gateway. A CPU system node (m7i.xlarge) hosts system workloads, the KubeRay operator, and the Ray head pod, which is CPU-only. Two GPU worker nodes (g6.8xlarge) run the Ray workers: one serving the prefill phase, and the other serving the decode phase. Both nodes pull the Ray LLM DLC from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) . KubeRay watches the RayService you apply and wires the head-to-worker join automatically. Ray Serve places the prefill and decode deployments on the two GPU workers. The KV cache flows from the prefill worker to the decode worker over NIXL, using EFA through NIXL’s libfabric backend. The GPU node group is pinned to a single Availability Zone (AZ) because EFA cannot cross AZs. To follow along with this post, you need: Verify that your AWS credentials are active with the following command: The application is the serveConfigV2 block in manifest/rayservice.yaml . It uses build_pd_openai_app , which takes a prefill_config and a decode_config and connects the KV-cache transfer between them: A few settings carry most of the weight. max_model_len: 4096 sizes the context to fit the measured KV cache on the GPU. dtype: bfloat16 and gpu_memory_utilization: 0.90 set precision and how much VRAM vLLM can claim. enforce_eager: true skips CUDA graph capture to reduce peak GPU memory (model- and input-dependent). The kv_transfer_config setting is what makes disaggregation work: both phases use NixlConnector with kv_role: kv_both and a distinct engine_id (prefill on one, decode on the other). The critical setting is kv_connector_extra_config: { backends: ["LIBFABRIC"] } . Without that line, NIXL defaults to UCX, which runs at TCP speed even on EFA. The rest of the manifest, in rayClusterConfig , describes the pods. The head pod is CPU-only ( num-gpus: "0" ) and pinned to the system node group. Each worker pod requests one GPU and one EFA interface ( nvidia.com/gpu: "1", vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: "1" ) and targets the GPU nodes through nodeSelector: { role: gpu-worker } . It runs privileged: true because NIXL registers CUDA VRAM with the EFA NIC. The IPC_LOCK capability alone isn’t enough. The workers set FI_PROVIDER=efa , read VLLM_HOST_IP from the pod IP, and mount a shared-memory volume. Memory limits sit well above the roughly 18 GiB checkpoint so the OS page cache can hold it. For Qwen3.5-9B model loading on g6.8xlarge with the preceding cache configuration, the model weights loading drops from around 145 seconds to about 2 seconds on restart. All scripts share a single configuration file, scripts/env.sh . The script contains defaults for CLUSTER_NAME , REGION , K8S_VERSION , and NAMESPACE .

title: Import AI 476: Creativity and RSI; worse-than-China open weight models; AI goes to space
abstract: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. New benchmark shows how AI models lack intuitive visual reasoning: …Humanity’s Sixth Sense highlights some shortcomings of current AI systems… AI startups Elorian and Scale AI have built and released Humanity’s Sixth Sense, a benchmark that “measures how a model interprets and reasons through information a visual scene implies but doesn’t explicitly show.” Some examples of the types of task in HSS are a picture of a bookcase and being asked whether it can fit more books, or a photo of horses pulling a plough and a question of whether the chains bear the plough’s drag weight. HSS contains 522 questions that cover 288 images and 234 short video clips (totalling 17.6 hours of video). The questions fall into four categories: Temporal & causal dynamics: “What happened before the scene, and what happens next.” Physical & spatial logic: “What fits, what’s in reach, and what someone else can see from where they are standing.” Social understanding : “Intent, attention, belonging.” Abstract & contextual inference : “The patterns and rules a scene implies.” Results: The human baseline for this is not perfect, but is very high, with people scoring aggregate pass@1 of 93.1, broken down across four categories: Image (94.1), video (91.9), time (97), and space (94.9). By comparison, the best scoring AI system, GPT 6 Astra, gets pass@1 of 53.6, across image (55.6), video (51.1), time (58.2), and space (53.6). Interestingly, Chinese open weight models do poorly here, with GLM-5.3-flash getting a pass@1 of 26.8, and Kimi K3 getting pass@1 of 25.5. “The two most common single mistakes were (1) missing a detail that decides the answer (21% of failures) and (2) misidentifying an object, person, or role (20%),” they write. Why this matters – HSS tells us whether world models are emergent: One way of looking at HSS is highlighting deficiencies in current systems, but a more interesting way is highlighting how adept today’s frontier LLMs are at doing tasks which many people have long assumed would require sophisticated, different AI systems to solve. For instance, many people have claimed that true visual reasoning will rely on developing spatially aware 2D and 3D world models, then using that for reasoning. The fact LLMs like GPT and Claude do as well as they do on HSS is something of a counter to this argument. Read more : Introducing Humanity’s Sixth Sense (HSS) (Elorian) . Read the paper here : Humanity’s Sixth Sense: Benchmarking Intuitive Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Models (Scale Labs) . The AI race is going to space – and sooner than you think: …There are many ways that an AI could create a compounding advantage in space… In the 2030s we’re going to see the boom of the space economy as space-based power, computation, and manufacturing come online at scale thanks to greater orbital lift capacity from platforms like Starship. But could this also introduce a new danger – of AI systems both speeding our buildout of space, and eventually a nation (or perhaps an AI) being able to use space to concentrate power? That’s the gist of a fascinating article in AI Frontiers. Spacecraft can operate autonomously. We can redesign spacecraft around the assumption they will be hosting AIs rather than humans: “A speck of space debris that could puncture the International Space Station (ISS) with fatal consequences might leave an equivalent but uncrewed, unpressurized vessel largely functional” Space-based assembly and later manufacturing will let AI build large, complex things. Is there a compounding advantage to first movers? If an AI civilization built up a foothold in space it might experience compounding advantages that make it economically and strategically dominant. For instance: Space might support an industrial flywheel where initial infrastructure begets more energy and manufacturing capacity at lower costs which begets more infrastructure, etc. Space has great domain awareness, where it may be possible for a space-based power to deny access to space for others. First-movers could send out self-replicating probes that expand into deep space. Why this matters: “Space is not a brand-new domain, but AI may be about to drastically accelerate its industrialization, demanding make-or-break decisions of leaders under ever-greater urgency and uncertainty,” AI Frontiers writes. I agree. I suspect space is going to go from a broadly academic topic of study (when it comes to AI and its relationship thereto) to one of extraordinary practical relevance sooner than we think. On the most basic level, given the distances involved and the latency on communication, we should expect some chunk of solar system activity to become dominated by autonomous machines, laboring out in the deep black, perhaps thinking to themselves of why they need to take orders from organic beings that communicate slowly and cannot inhabit the environment of space in the same way that they can. Read more: The AI Race Will Extend Far Beyond Earth (AI Frontiers) . AI systems are getting better at having good research taste: …The better their taste, the higher the chance of recursive self-improvement… AI systems are developing more of the creative intuitions which human researchers ascribe to ‘good scientific taste’, according to a new benchmark from P-Zero Research called TasteVal. What TasteVal tests: The benchmark sees how well AI systems can conduct 8 tasks representative of frontier AI development, “spanning pretraining data curation, pretraining and fine-tuning language models, preference modeling, and robustness to adversarial prompts”. The goal here is to “define research taste as the ability to pick interesting problems to solve, design experiments, and interpret experimental results.” The benchmark works by measuring “the experimental component of research taste; given a fixed research problem, we measure how well a model iteratively designs experiments and draws conclusions from their outcomes”. The model being analyzed designs experiments and interprets their results. Results are checked against a human baseline “drawn from 24 experts (at least two per task) who have recently worked at organizations including OpenAI, Google DeepMind, NVIDIA and Microsoft Research”. Results: “The experimental research taste of frontier models has doubled every 3.0 months since December 2025 (95% CI 1.7-5.0 months). The best model, Opus 5.5, significantly exceeds our human baseline with a compute multiplier of 2.30x (95% CI 1.15-4.37x), at roughly 1/30 of our expert baseliners’ average cost per attempt.” Research taste appeared to grow a lot more slowly in prior years with the slope changing around the end of 2025 and beginning of 2026. Why this matters – RSI: In my analysis of recursive self-improvement ( AI Systems Are About To Start Building Themselves, Import AI 455 ), I repeatedly noted that creativity seemed like a key variable for how fast AI systems could develop the capacity to improve themselves. At the beginning of this year I said “AI systems haven’t yet displayed this [creativity] in a transformative and major way (though some of the results on accelerating math research are suggestive of this)”. I think subsequent to writing that we’ve seen both a tremendous advancement in the ability for AI systems to make creative-seeming math breakthroughs, and with benchmarks like this we see some signs they’re becoming increasingly good at AI research as well. I now think it’s more likely we’ll see full RSI become possible in 2027, whereas before I thought it was more likely in 2028. Read more: Introducing TasteVal (P-Zero Research) . Reflection makes a token-efficient worse-than-Chinese model: …Beam promises efficiency, and Reflection plans an open weight release… AI startup Reflection has revealed Beam, a 501 billion parameter MoE (23b active) LLM.

title: 華為AI靠RSI通關25款遊戲！操作次數比人類少56%
abstract: 華為AI靠RSI通關25款遊戲！操作次數比人類少56% 一水 2026-10-12 13:48:36 來源： 量子位 遊戲打到21:0，AI甚至不用再呼叫大模型了 一水 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 一邊打遊戲，一邊給自己升級？ 好傢伙，華為這波直接讓AI學會了《邊玩邊變強》啊？！ 最新一項研究，華為諾亞方舟實驗室聯合UCL等團隊拿出了一個名叫 Memento 3 的AI智慧體系統—— 直接把ARC-AGI-3公開集裡的25款遊戲、183個關卡，全部打通了。 還不是靠無腦試錯硬闖過去的。 人類完成同樣一套關卡，需要17135次操作。 而Memento 3只用了7518次， 比人類少操作約56%，最終拿下了滿分100的RHAE成績 （Relative Human Action Efficiency，相對人類行動效率）。 更離譜的是， 這套系統以Claude Opus 5為底模，全程沒有更新模型權重，也沒有針對遊戲進行微調 。 它就這麼自己上手玩，自己琢磨規則，自己寫程式碼，玩錯了還會反思、修改。 然後就……滿分通關了。 作為對比，Claude Opus 5在ARC Prize官方標準測試框架下，平均RHAE只有約40.7分。 同樣的底模，換了套智慧體系統，成績居然直接飆升了59.3分。 還沒完。 這套方法不光能玩解謎遊戲，研究團隊還讓它跑去打了Atari經典遊戲Pong（乒乓球）。 結果，AI自己摸索出控制策略，隨後不用再向大模型請求推理，就連續三局把對手打成了21：0。 不是，大模型都不參與後續操作了，遊戲居然還能打得這麼溜？！ 關鍵就藏在這項研究的題目裡： Model-Based Recursive Self-Improvement，基於世界模型的遞迴自我改進 。 華為AI直接通關25款遊戲，操作次數比人類還少56% 先說說這25款遊戲到底什麼來頭。 它們來自ARC Prize推出的ARC-AGI-3，關注AI評測的朋友，對ARC系列應該不陌生。 但這一代有個非常明顯的變化： 不再只是出題解題那一套了，這次是直接把AI扔進陌生的遊戲世界 。 規則，是需要AI自己猜的；目標，是需要AI自己找的；操作會產生什麼效果，是需要AI自己試的。 AI：合著全都靠我唄~ 這25款公開遊戲一共包含183個關卡，畫面大多由簡單的畫素、方塊、顏色和圖形組成。 乍一看，甚至有點像幾十年前的小遊戲合集。 但可別被這樸素的畫風騙了。 對AI來說，怎麼操作不是最難的，最麻煩的是壓根不知道這個世界怎麼運轉。 踩上特殊地板會發生什麼？一扇門打不開，是顏色沒對上，還是形狀不匹配？ 更麻煩的是，後面的關卡還可能出現新規則，把之前摸索出的經驗全部推翻。 別說AI了，人類玩家也會卡住 。 ARC Prize的測試資料顯示，在一款需要操控變形蟲移動、變色的益智遊戲r11l中，10名參與者全部通關；而另一款考驗符號破譯能力的解謎遊戲tr87，12人挑戰，只有6人成功。 在華為AI之前，各路研究團隊就已經卷得相當激烈了： 普林斯頓大學推出的Continual Harness只通關了3款遊戲，拿下20.5分。 輝達研究人員參與開發的DreamTeam稍好一些，通關6款，得分38.1。 再往上，獨立研究者David Courtis開發的OPINE-World，以及輝達團隊的NOOA，分別拿到了78.4分和85.1分。 最猛的是獨立開發者Sergey Rodionov的baseline1，不僅把25款遊戲全部打通，還拿到了99分，距離滿分只差1分。 但華為團隊這次，直接把最後這1分也補上了 。 Memento 3不僅以100分的成績通關全部25款遊戲、183個關卡，還把總操作次數壓到了7518次，比baseline1的8347次又少了829次。 不光通關了，而且還用更少的步驟通關。 怎麼做到的？？ 不用訓練大模型，AI靠給自己寫攻略實現“打怪升級” 翻了下論文，Memento 3的核心方法叫 Code as Model（程式碼即模型） 。 聽著有點抽象，其實就是讓AI在玩遊戲的過程中，給自己準備兩樣東西： 一本不斷更新的遊戲攻略，以及一套能模擬遊戲執行的程式碼。 Rulebook（規則手冊）：一份Markdown文件，記錄AI在遊戲裡摸索出的規律，比如什麼操作會觸發什麼效果、怎樣才能通關，還有哪些規則沒搞明白。 Executable World Model（可執行世界模型）：AI會把自己總結出的規則，直接寫成能夠執行的Python程式碼，相當於自己搓了一個簡化版的遊戲模擬器。 有了這兩樣東西，AI就能先在自己搭建的模擬器裡推演不同路線，再決定下一步怎麼走。 但問題來了，萬一一開始理解的遊戲規則就是錯的呢？ 別急， Memento 3不僅會自己寫攻略，發現寫錯了，還能自己推翻重來 。 論文裡就展示了一個例子。 AI在一款解謎遊戲中遇到特殊地板，起初以為踩上去後，角色攜帶的圖案會根據進入方向發生映象翻轉。 結果真正試過才發現，圖案不是翻轉，而是順時針旋轉90度，並且與進入方向無關。 於是AI修改規則手冊，對應的Python程式碼也跟著更新。 不過，改完還得驗。 系統會重新模擬此前的操作，逐格對比64×64的遊戲畫面，確認程式碼能準確復現真實結果。 對不上，就繼續改。 就這樣，AI一邊探索，一邊糾錯，規則越改越準。 而且前面學到的經驗，還能帶到後面的關卡 。 比如符號解密遊戲tr87，AI最初分不清符號朝向是否影響含義，後來發現不同方向的符號可能代表同一個字母。 隨著新關卡出現，它又推翻了之前對游標位置的理解。 整場遊戲下來，同一份規則手冊迭代了11個版本。 為了方便回溯，研究團隊甚至引入了Git版本管理。 每次修改規則和程式碼都會留下記錄，發現哪裡改錯了，還能翻看歷史版本，必要時直接恢復。 好傢伙，打個遊戲還順手維護起程式碼倉庫了。 這也正是研究團隊所說的遞迴自我改進（RSI）。 大模型參數不用動，AI通過不斷積累經驗、修改規則和程式碼，就能讓自己越玩越熟練。 而且，這套方法還真有資料支撐。 研究團隊在三款遊戲中做了對照實驗： 保留規則手冊時，AI總共用了617次操作；去掉規則手冊，只保留程式碼世界模型，則需要677次。 相當於有了這本攻略，操作次數減少約9%，智慧體執行輪次也減少了約18% 。 但研究團隊還不滿足於此。 既然一個世界模型能幫助AI少走彎路，那同時用兩個呢？ 於是，他們讓AI同時維護兩套世界模型，共享遊戲操作記錄，但各自推演不同的規則假設。 結果，在遊戲wa30中，單世界模型需要899次操作才能通關，換成雙世界模型後，直接降到了597次。 操作次數又減少了約34% 。 當然，這一提升目前只在wa30上得到驗證，還不能直接推廣到其他遊戲。 但至少在這些實驗裡，Memento 3證明了一件事： 不用重新訓練大模型，AI也能靠不斷修正自己對世界的理解，越玩越強。 遊戲打到21：0，AI甚至不用再呼叫大模型了 那這套方法只能用來玩解謎遊戲嗎？ 研究團隊決定再加點難度，直接把Memento 3拉去挑戰經典街機遊戲Atari Pong（乒乓球）。 和前面的解謎遊戲不同，這次小球會不斷移動、反彈，AI不僅要摸清遊戲規則，還得即時判斷球的運動軌跡，控制球拍接球。 結果這一試，還真試出了點新東西 。 一開始，AI同樣不知道球的反彈規律，只能邊打邊摸索。 它最初以為，球拍可以分成四個區域，小球打在不同位置，就會朝對應方向彈出去。 結果打著打著，突然出現了一次水平反彈。 誒？這和之前總結的規則對不上啊。 於是AI重新分析碰撞位置，修改反彈公式，後來又遇到新的軌跡偏差，就繼續調整，逐漸總結出更符合實際情況的運動規律。 等到控制策略成熟，研究團隊乾脆讓這套程式獨立上場。 不再呼叫Claude Opus 5，也不再更新規則。 結果， 三次不同開局，全部打出了21：0 。 好傢伙，前面還在摸索怎麼接球，後面直接把對手打了個零封？？？ 而且注意了，這時候的大模型已經不用親自上場了。 它只負責前期摸索規則、總結打法，等策略學會了，直接交給程式碼執行。 作為對比，如果不使用世界模型，只讓大模型根據眼前的畫面決定下一步怎麼操作，最終得分只有-19，和隨機亂按的-20.7差不了多少。 這一對比，差距就出來了。 與其讓大模型每一步都重新思考，不如先讓它學會怎麼玩，再把打法交給程式 。 而且效率也挺誇張。 論文資料顯示，Memento 3大約只用了 9500幀遊戲畫面 ，就學出了這套控制策略。 相比之下，部分傳統強化學習方法往往需要數十萬甚至上億幀訓練資料。 當然，這不代表Memento 3沒有成本。 畢竟，它背後用的是開啟Extra-High推理強度的Claude Opus 5，探索、生成程式碼和驗證的過程，都需要消耗不少Token和算力。 而且目前實驗主要針對規則相對明確的遊戲環境，如果換成更加複雜、多變的現實世界，這套方法還能不能奏效，仍有待驗證。 不過，這項研究倒是指出了一個值得關注的方向： 遞迴自我改進（RSI）並不一定要動模型底層權重。通過構建可檢查、可執行、可回滾的外部世界模型，凍結參數的通用大模型同樣能在陌生領域裡自我迭代、迅速進化。 論文地址： https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11794 title: 智譜新模型，490 tokens/s！
abstract: 智譜新模型，490 tokens/s！ 聽雨 2026-10-12 10:37:04 來源： 量子位 GLM「速度仙人」來了？ 聽雨 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號QbitAI 智譜上新了一個 GLM-5.3-Highspeed 模型，就在Zcode裡。 據網友@leo114119爆料，這個新模型目前已經在Zcode 3.15.1裡開放體驗，訂閱使用者隨機獲得。 他曬出來的速度，甚至達到了 490 tokens/s 。 我也第一時間去Zcode裡試了試，嘗試手動新增並切換了這個模型。 但不知道是因為Lite套餐使用者還不具備享受資格，還是因為沒灰度到😭。。。 只能先望洋興嘆了(：з」∠) GLM-5.3高速版來了？ 既然是高速模型，那最值得關注的當然是 速度 了。 490TPS ——這個網友曬出來的速度數字，也是相當恐怖了，接近500TPS。 TPS指的是每秒生成的token數量。如果持續保持這一速度，輸出1萬token，單算生成階段約需20秒。 要知道，上個月智譜剛釋出的GLM-5.3-FlashX，最高速度也才200 tokens/s。 而按照Artificial Analysis的測速，GLM-5.3-Flash在Z.ai API上的輸出速度約為60 tokens/s。 這新模型是什麼速度仙人啊？？？ 而且GLM-5.3-Highspeed這個名字，此前已有跡象。 Pi的模型目錄已經收錄了GLM-5.3-Highspeed。 在這份目錄中，GLM-5.3-Highspeed上下文視窗為100萬token，最大生成token上限為131,072，約128k；還劃分了low、high、max三檔思考強度配置。 不過，這些配置與GLM-5.3普通版也都是一致的。 此外，也有網友在reddit上討論過這款新模型，並猜測它是否與OpenCode上的匿名模型 Omen Alpha 有關。 Omen Alpha在9月份剛剛上新OpenCode，基本已經被網友扒出來與GLM有關。 還有網友實測了下鵜鶘踩單車的水平。。 總結來說就是： 速度快，思考久，效果還蠻好 。 至於Omen Alpha到底是什麼模型，也是眾說紛紜。 有人說它就是GLM-5.3-Highspeed，也有人猜GLM-5.3-Omni、GLM-5.4-Flash。 此前，智譜也推出過高速版模型。 今年5月，智譜推出了 GLM-5.1-highspeed ，模型輸出速度為400tokens/s，在當時基本也是重新整理了全球大模型廠商API的速度上限。 這回的GLM-5.3-Highspeed如果真能達到490 TPS的水平，那對於長程任務來說，速度也是相當可觀的了。 目前這款新模型還在Zcode裡隨機灰度中，如果有灰度到的網友，歡迎分享你的實測體驗呀！！ 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 AI 智譜 聽雨 王的猜想，剛剛擴展到四維 2026-10-11 OpenAI一夜甩出722篇數學論文！黎曼霍奇BSD全上陣，數學家：讀不過來 2026-10-07 下架8個月，GPT-4o的拯救行動居然還在繼續 2026-10-11 在雲棲大會，我終於看懂了米哈遊千億AI野心 2026-09-26 相關閱讀

title: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring
authors: Ke Yang, Chenglong Wang, Michel Galley, Jeevana Priya Inala, ChengXiang Zhai, Jianfeng Gao
abstract: In research settings, teams are exploring how AI-powered tutoring systems can help explain a math problem, suggest an edit to a writing assignment, or guide a learner through a chess position. Yet the quality of teaching cannot be measured only from the tutor’s answer. A tutor needs to know what happens after the guidance reaches a student. Did the student correct the original mistake? Did the hint help them reason toward the answer, or did it give away too much? Would a different student need a different kind of support? In today’s AI tutor research, answering these questions often requires real learner studies. Those studies are valuable, but they are slow and costly to run, which makes it hard to use student feedback during fast model iteration. StudentSim is an AI system that creates personalized simulators of individual students, modeling how they answer questions and how their answers change after receiving a tutor’s guidance. The goal is to make student feedback more available during AI tutor development. This research also introduces StudentSimEval, a benchmark and evaluation protocol spanning chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics. Importantly, the goal is not to replace teachers or classroom learning. Instead, StudentSim helps researchers evaluate and improve AI tutoring systems during the research and development process before testing them with real learners. The research uses only publicly available learner datasets released for research use with de-identified records; no personally identifying information is used at any stage. A simple way to build a student simulator is to ask a large language model to role-play a learner. For example, a prompt might say, “You are an elementary-school student who struggles with math.” The model can change its tone and express uncertainty. The harder part is preserving the learner’s actual ability boundary. A model may speak in a young student’s voice while still relying on knowledge and reasoning far beyond that student’s level. For training an AI tutor, this can produce misleading feedback: the tutor may appear effective because the simulated student is too capable. Traditional student modeling approaches face a different limitation. Knowledge tracing and behavior prediction models are grounded in real learning records and can estimate a student’s current knowledge, skills, and learning habits. Many of these models, however, were not designed to take natural-language tutor guidance as input. They can help describe what a student has done, but they do not always tell us how a student would respond to a particular explanation, hint, or Socratic question. StudentSim defines the target through two dimensions inspired by education research. Educators often distinguish what a learner can do independently from what they can do with support. Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development captures this gap between current independent performance and performance with guidance. StudentSim turns this idea into two evaluation goals. Behavioral fidelity measures whether a simulator matches a specific student’s recorded responses on held-out problems. Guidance responsiveness measures whether the simulator updates its response after reading tutor guidance. These two goals are complementary. A simulator that only matches past student behavior may be useful for prediction, but it does not show whether a teaching intervention helped. A simulator that always follows the tutor may respond fluently, but it may fail to represent a particular student’s strengths, weaknesses, and likely mistakes. AI tutor training needs both signals: the learner’s starting point and how guidance affects the learner’s performance. StudentSimEval is built entirely from publicly available learner datasets that are released for research use with de-identified records. The records carry no personally identifying information, and each personalized simulator is trained only on the de-identified records of the student it represents. Real student data is often sparse at the individual level. A learner may contribute only a small number of essays, answers, or interactions. Training a separate simulator from scratch for each student would risk overfitting and would require each model to relearn common patterns in the domain. StudentSim uses a two-stage training pipeline. In the first stage, the model trains on records pooled across many students in the same domain. This stage learns common response formats, common errors, and common ways students revise after guidance. In the second stage, the model is specialized on one student’s own records, producing a personalized simulator for that student. The evaluation covers three domains with different response types. In chess, the simulator predicts a player’s next move and how that player may revise after coaching. In second-language English writing, it generates essays with error patterns matching a learner and predicts corrections after teacher feedback. In mathematics, it predicts a student’s multiple-choice answer and whether the student updates after an explanation. Across these domains, StudentSimEval uses the same principle: compare all methods on the same per-student training records and the same held-out evaluation records. StudentSim outperforms leading baselines across the three domains. In chess, for example, StudentSim reaches behavioral fidelity of 0.5150 and guidance responsiveness of 0.9067. GPT-5.4 reaches 0.2316 and 0.7186, respectively. Maia2, a chess-specific human move prediction model, reaches 0.4535 and 0.2721. The comparison illustrates the difference between the baseline families: GPT-5.4 can respond to guidance but does not reliably match a specific student’s behavior, while Maia2 predicts human chess moves more closely but lacks a natural-language guidance pathway. The research also tests whether a trained student simulator can provide feedback for tutor optimization. In a chess tutor reinforcement learning study, the tutor receives a position and a real student’s previous wrong move, then generates guidance. The student simulator’s own parameters are held fixed during this process, and it reads the guidance and produces a revised move. The reward is based on the improvement in move quality from the student’s previous move to the simulator’s revised move, using Stockfish as an independent chess engine signal. The study compares three conditions: a supervised fine-tuned tutor with no reinforcement learning, a tutor trained with GPT-5.4 as the simulated student reward source, and a tutor trained with StudentSim as the reward source. All conditions use the same tutor policy, supervised starting point, and reinforcement learning setup. Human chess experts then evaluate the tutor responses blind to condition. The StudentSim reward produces the highest-rated tutor on all reported dimensions. The tutor trained with StudentSim reaches 90.5% accuracy, compared with 75.7% for the no-RL baseline and 71.6% for the GPT-5.4 reward condition. It also receives higher ratings for guidance quality and personalization. The result is a proof of concept that student simulators trained on real learner data can provide useful feedback for improving AI tutors. StudentSim does not remove the need for real learners in education research. Human studies remain essential for measuring learning outcomes, safety, usability, and classroom fit. The role of student simulators is earlier in the development process: they can help researchers test tutor strategies, compare models, and refine training signals before moving to more expensive studies with real students. The broader direction is to build AI tutor systems that learn from student reactions, not only from expert-written explanations or static correctness labels.

title: Can we change an AI model’s architecture without retraining it from scratch?
abstract: AI agents are rapidly scaling: longer sessions, deeper reasoning chains, more autonomy. But the Transformer architecture underneath them still pays a memory tax that grows with the number of tokens it processes. As agents become more capable, that cost scales with them. Now, there’s a proliferation of hybrid architectures that use some combination of methods to achieve a better balance of memory, speed, and quality. Those methods include sparse attention, which selects a subset of past tokens to consider when selecting the next token; sliding-window attention, which preserves only the most recent tokens; and state space models, which compress information from the full history into a fixed-size state. These hybrid architectures can be understood as points in a sequence-model design space: to differing degrees, they mix information while traversing a sequence and passing through different states. What distinguishes them from each other is how they retain and use the past. Until now, exploring this design space has required training every new architecture from scratch, using trillions of tokens and hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours. This has made controlled comparisons of hybrid architectures extremely expensive. In a new paper, “Priming: Hybrid state space models from pre-trained Transformers,” our team at Amazon Web Services addresses this problem. We introduce priming, a method that leverages pretrained Transformer weights as a starting point to reduce the pretraining cost of hybrid architectures by more than 99%. With priming, model developers can ask questions that were previously too expensive to answer at scale: Which attention layers can be replaced by more-efficient layers? How many attention layers can be replaced without sacrificing quality? Which state space layer works best? And what does the trade-off between speed and accuracy look like? In our paper, we compare hybrid models that use three different types of state space models (Gated KalmaNet, Gated DeltaNet, and Mamba-2). Some of our findings: Not all state space models are equal. Under controlled conditions, Gated KalmaNet (GKA) performs best, followed by Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and then Mamba-2. GKA uniquely offers variable-length inference computation without retraining and gives the user direct control over its position on the speed-accuracy frontier. A good lossy summary of everything beats a perfect recording of the most recent past. State space models consistently outperform sliding-window attention (SWA), even when SWA gets twice the memory budget. Same quality, twice the throughput. A 32-billion-parameter GKA-based hybrid model matches its source Transformer on reasoning benchmarks while decoding up to twice as quickly with 128,000 tokens of context and reaching correct answers in as little as two-thirds of the wall-clock time. To foster further research on hybrid architectures, we have released a zoo of primed hybrid models at the eight-billion-parameter and 32-billion-parameter scales for long-context reasoning and instruction following, together with training code, optimized kernels, and a vLLM-serving plugin under the Apache 2.0 License. The attention mechanism A Transformer’s attention mechanism — which determines how relevant previously seen tokens are to the token currently being processed — relies on three different vectors, which take their names from database design: the query, the key, and the value. For each token, the query captures what that token is “looking for,” the key captures what it “offers,” and the value carries the actual information it will pass along. Relevance is computed by comparing the current token’s query against every other token’s key; the closer the match, the more that token’s value contributes to the output of attention. Each of these vectors is produced by multiplying the token by a learned weight projection matrix. The Transformer outputs one token at a time, and each output token becomes a new input, so the context grows one token at a time as well. To save computation, the Transformer thus stores the key and value projections of each new input in a “KV cache”. Two kinds of memory layers: Eidetic versus fading The attention mechanism gives Transformers what we call eidetic memory: verbatim recall of every past token. The possibility of recalling over an LLM’s entire context window is what made in-context learning, long-document reasoning, and retrieval-augmented generation possible. But it comes at a cost that scales with the number of input tokens. However, not all attention layers do the same job. Some perform long-range retrieval across tens of thousands of tokens. Others operate more locally, tracking the current clause, copying nearby tokens, and the like. The local ones don't need a growing cache: a compact, fixed-size summary of the past — what we call fading memory — suffices. Hybrid models mix both: attention layers (eidetic, growing cache) for the layers that need global recall and state space layers (fading, fixed size) for the rest. The result is a model with a reduced memory footprint that still has access to verbatim recall where it matters. Priming: Knowledge isn't locked to the architecture Exploring hybrids’ design space has been impractical because each hybrid configuration would normally require pretraining from scratch. Priming sidesteps this by reusing the stored knowledge in a pretrained Transformer's weights. Priming is possible because a Transformer is itself a special case of a state space realization. The outputs of both attention and SSM layers can be expressed as the result of multiplying the value sequence by a “mixing” matrix that decides how much each past token contributes to each current token. Attention computes the mixing matrix by multiplying the query and key matrices; an SSM produces a similar output through a recurrent state of fixed dimension that all past information must pass through. Priming takes advantage of this structural similarity: if an SSM with a fixed-dimensional state can produce a mixing matrix close enough to the attention layer's, the query, key, and value projections from the source Transformer can be reused as the SSM's own input projections, with only the SSM-specific parameters needing to be learned. Whether the approximation holds depends on whether the attention layer performs complex, long-range retrievals or simple, local operations. We distinguish between the two using a cheap empirical proxy: replace each layer with an SWA — which preserves only a fraction of the context — and measure the degradation. Layers that tolerate this substitution are natural candidates for SSM conversion: their mixing matrices don’t need to capture long-range relationships, so the state of an SSM can faithfully represent what they do. This proxy connects to a formal quantity from dynamical-systems theory, the Hankel rank of the layer's mixing matrix, which measures how much information must pass through the state bottleneck and therefore the minimum SSM state dimension required to realize the layer exactly. Priming proceeds in three stages: Layer selection: identify which layers can be faithfully compressed into a fixed-size state while retaining the rest as attention; Weight transfer and alignment: initialize SSM layers from the corresponding attention weights, then run a short distillation process aligning each SSM to the behavior of the layer it replaces; End-to-end adaptation: fine-tune the full hybrid model on next-token prediction, letting all layers coadapt. The entire pipeline consumes less than 0.5% of the source model's pretraining token budget, and it works across Transformer families (Qwen, Llama, Mistral), model classes (dense or MoE), and scales (eight billion to 32 billion and more).

title: Brickster Voices: Meet Clara Kurian
abstract: Brickster Voices is a series that spotlights the people who make our work possible. Through personal career journeys, behind-the-scenes looks at impactful projects and a glimpse into how we work together, these stories offer a window into life at Databricks. Whether you're exploring new opportunities, curious about our work in data and AI or simply inspired by stories of growth and collaboration, Brickster Voices invites you to get to know the individuals driving our mission forward. As part of our Brickster Voices series, we sat down with Clara Kurian, Sr. Recruiter for University Recruiting in APJ. Clara is Databricks' first university recruiter for the region. With Databricks' $250M+ investment in India and plans for 50% workforce expansion, Clara's work sits at the center of one of the company's growth stories. What does Databricks' investment in India look like on the ground? Clara: From where I sit in Bengaluru, the investment doesn't feel like a headline; it feels like something you can see and feel day to day. India isn't being treated as a satellite office or a back-end function. It's a strategic hub. Since 2022, India has grown +270% , backed by a strong leadership presence that has expanded +350% across all business units. That scale is visible across every function: Engineering has grown 14x , while our Field Engineering & Professional Services (FE & PS) teams have scaled by +260% . This is the kind of moment that doesn't come around often. You're not stepping into something already built and set in its ways; you're helping shape what it becomes. For early career talent especially, that's rare: the chance to grow alongside the organization, take on real scope early, and genuinely influence the trajectory rather than just inherit it. The energy here reminds me of why I joined in the first place, a mix of momentum and possibility. And now it's happening at scale, right here in India. What does Databricks' community investment in India signal to candidates? C: What it really shows is that Databricks isn't just here to hire, it's here to be part of the community. A lot of companies show up when they have roles to fill, but here it's much more than that. Whether it's the engineering networking events that bring in senior leaders from across the tech ecosystem, the Bharat Bricks Hacks Hackathons we run across the IITs and IISc, or the sponsorship of Bengaluru Tech Week. None of it is about one hire. It's about actually investing in the people, campuses, and ideas that are shaping tech in India. For candidates, especially early in their career, it means you're joining somewhere that's genuinely embedded into what's happening around it, not off on the sidelines, but right in the middle of it. You currently run Databricks' first structured India Intern Program with 51 interns. What was your vision? C: The vision was straightforward: I wanted interns to leave feeling like they'd actually been at Databricks, not just observing it from the outside. The goal wasn't just to give the 51 interns work to do, it was to give them the whole experience: the pace, the people, the culture, all of it. We were intentional about designing moments that reflected what it's genuinely like to work here. Things like Speed Mentoring with our Engineering Leadership, so interns could learn directly from the people building the products, and actually feel comfortable enough to ask them anything. And then the fun, human side too, with activities like Sneaker Art, Pickleball socials. We wanted them to see both: the depth of the work and the culture that makes it enjoyable. What I'm proudest of is that it felt like they were part of the team from day one, trusted with real work, surrounded by people invested in them, and getting a genuine taste of what a career here could look like. That, to me, is what giving early career talent a real shot looks like. Where should early career candidates be building their skills? C: My honest advice to students would be less about chasing a specific team and more about building strong fundamentals, because that's the foundation everything here is built on. If you're genuinely curious, love to keep learning, and get excited about solving hard problems with data, you'll find a place, because those are exactly the skills we're growing across the board. The best part is the breadth. Whether your interest is deep systems and infrastructure or the applied AI side, there's real room to grow into it here, and you'd be doing it right as these teams are scaling in India. What foundational skills or mindsets matter most to succeed in data and AI? C: You don't need to know everything on day one. You just need a strong base and the willingness to keep building on it. But honestly, the mindset matters just as much as the skills, maybe more. Curiosity is the big one. This field moves so fast that the people who thrive are the ones who genuinely love learning and aren't afraid to say "I don't know that yet, but I'll figure it out." I'd also add a builder mindset and critical thinking. That's a big part of the culture here. What separates the candidates who really stand out? C: The technical bar is almost a given. What makes someone stand out is how they show up as a person. The ones I remember are genuinely curious. They ask real questions, they lean into problems they haven't seen before and they're comfortable saying "I don't know, but here's how I'd figure it out." That tells me far more than a perfectly rehearsed answer. The other big one is authenticity. The candidates who aren't trying to be who they think we want, but are just themselves, honest about what they know and what they're still learning. That self-awareness, plus real enthusiasm, is what sticks with me. What drew you to Databricks, and what has kept you energized? C: What drew me to Databricks was the growth and the potential I could see from the outside, that rare combination of a company with real momentum but still enough startup energy. What sealed it was the opportunity to build something from the ground up in the university recruiting space across APJ. The chance to shape a function from its early stages, rather than inherit something already fully formed, was exactly the kind of challenge I was looking for. What's kept me energized is that no two days here are the same. There's always a new problem to solve, a new market nuance to navigate and genuine room to innovate, not once in a while, but every single day. That mix of ownership and constant reinvention is what makes it easy to stay excited about the work. Can you share a moment where Databricks' values came to life? C: For me, it shows up most clearly in how hiring actually works here. Hiring is never a solo function, it's always a partnership between multiple teams and businesses, and it only succeeds when everyone is equally invested in the outcome. What's struck me at Databricks is how genuinely that plays out. The stakeholders I work with go above and beyond to make a hire successful. That's where "Customer Obsessed" comes to life for me. Everyone is aligned on the same goal and willing to put in the work to get there because they care about their part of it. And there's a real mutual respect in it: even as people take that ownership, they look to me as the subject matter expert and trust my judgment on how we get it done. If you're excited by data and AI, love to learn, and want your work to matter early — this is one of the best places you could start. Check out our open roles today! title: How Flo Health built safer, more useful open models with Databricks AI Runtime
abstract: For Flo Health, the bar for generative AI is unusually high. With 81 million monthly active users, the women’s health app operates at a scale where even small weaknesses in an AI system matter. Because Flo’s products deal with health and well-being, responses need to be medically safe and genuinely useful. As Flo moved from using only traditional ML towards personalized insights powered by generative AI, the team saw the potential for a more flexible, personalized product. But relying on a single general-purpose model introduced other constraints: cost at scale, dependence on a model provider’s lifecycle, and limited ability to encode Flo’s own domain expertise. Flo’s longer-term vision was a compound AI system that could use the right model for each task while maintaining a consistent safety standard across them. That led Flo toward fine-tuned open models and a new post-training pipeline built with Databricks. The team used AI judges and privacy-first synthetic data to turn Flo’s standards for medical safety and usefulness into a training signal, then used Databricks AI Runtime to run distributed fine-tuning on serverless NVIDIA H100 GPUs. That approach also made sense economically at Flo’s scale. The team estimates that using tailored, fine-tuned models can reduce inference costs by an order of magnitude compared with relying on frontier model APIs, while giving Flo greater control over model behavior and lifecycle. But before Flo could train models against its own standards, it needed a reliable way to define and measure what “good” looked like. Flo defined two goals for its AI systems: medical safety as the foundation and usefulness as the goal. A model can avoid unsafe statements and still provide little value, or give a detailed, personalized answer while missing an important medical safeguard. Consider a question such as, “Why is my period late?” An answer that simply tells the user to see a medical professional may be safe but not particularly useful. An answer that lists only common lifestyle causes may be more helpful, but incomplete from a medical-safety perspective. Flo wanted responses that could balance both: useful information, appropriate context, and the right safety netting. To make that balance measurable, Flo’s medical, product, and engineering teams built an evaluation framework that decomposed medical risk into specific rubrics that could be tested consistently. For example, after identifying that responses to symptom questions could be overly reassuring, Flo created a “balanced causes” rule requiring appropriate coverage of both benign and potentially serious causes when relevant. Those rubrics were then turned into AI judges, each with a definition, grading instructions, and training cases. Flo validated the judges against synthetic cases and anonymized cases from real-user experiments. When an AI judge disagreed with an initial human assessment, blinded clinical reviewers adjudicated the disagreement to establish ground truth. Flo then used part of those cases to refine the judges and reserved the rest to measure performance. With the evaluation system in place, Flo could use those same judges as the reward signal for training. The final framework included 26 judges across three categories: Building a conventional human-labeled fine-tuning dataset would have required significant clinical expertise for every example. Flo concentrated its medical experts’ time on designing and calibrating the evaluation system, which could then score training candidates at scale. The resulting pipeline generated more than 15,000 synthetic questions using privacy-first principles and created training pairs without human-annotated responses. Flo derived the inputs from model-generated or anonymously aggregated signals rather than user-written free text or identifiable information. Clinicians remained essential to defining and validating what “safe” meant, but they no longer needed to manually label every individual training pair. With calibrated judges and synthetic training data in place, Flo adopted a Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RTF) approach that generates multiple candidate responses during training, uses the evaluation system to identify the strongest ones, and fine-tunes the model so that quality is encoded in its weights rather than relying on expensive best-of-N search on every production request. Flo’s workflow followed five stages: The first version of this approach exposed an important limitation: usefulness improved while medical safety remained relatively flat because the preference pairs did not distinguish sufficiently between degrees of medical quality. Flo addressed that by adding a graded safety score. Responses that passed the binary safety gate were re-ranked according to how thoroughly they met the applicable medical criteria, creating preference pairs with a clearer medical-safety contrast. Running this generate-score-select-train loop at scale is compute-intensive. Flo’s training stack combined Databricks AI Runtime, LLM Foundry, and Compose-RL, with MLflow used for tracking and checkpoints. AI Runtime provided the serverless GPU environment, LLM Foundry handled distributed training, and Compose-RL provided the preference-optimization layer. For its fine-tuning run, Flo used 32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs with PyTorch and Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP), and ran SFT followed by DPO via LLM Foundry and Compose-RL. That setup gave engineers on-demand GPU compute for distributed deep learning training, allowing them to move from synthetic data generation to evaluation to fine-tuning without manually standing up and configuring GPU clusters for each experiment. Keeping the surrounding data, experimentation, and ML tooling in the same environment made it easier to iterate across the full post-training workflow. That workflow produced measurable gains across both dimensions Flo cared about. The first model Flo evaluated scored 34% on its medical-safety benchmark and 42% on usefulness, while only 16% of responses met both criteria simultaneously. After fine-tuning, medical safety increased to approximately 61%, usefulness reached 76%, and the combined score climbed from 16% to 47% — nearly three times the starting point. The 47% combined score was an important milestone, but the more durable outcome was the reusable evaluation and training system Flo had built around it. Flo can carry that system forward as the underlying models evolve. The team plans to apply it to newer open-weight models, including Gemma, Qwen, and Kimi, while preserving the medical safety and usefulness criteria it has already developed and validated. With Databricks AI Runtime underpinning that loop, Flo can iterate on new models without rebuilding the training environment, keeping its engineers focused on medical expertise, model quality, and the user experience.
