title: How distributed inference keeps large AI models moving
abstract: When an AI model answers a question or completes a task, it performs inference, i.e., using a trained model to generate an output in response to some input. Doing that at scale, however, is more challenging than it sounds. Running a large language model on a GPU is one thing. Serving that model to thousands or even millions of people and AI agents at the same time is quite another. Requests arrive with different priorities and lengths, which have unique computing needs. Some users expect an immediate response to simple queries, while others submit large jobs that can run in the background. AI agent traffic adds a new pattern: Agents may send bursts of related requests, pause to call a tool, and then return with nearly the same context. Meanwhile, the system must make efficient use of expensive accelerators without creating long queues or repeatedly performing the same computations. This challenge resembles air traffic control. A busy airport cannot simply send each arriving aircraft to the first available runway. Controllers in the tower must account for the aircraft’s location, destination, size, and fuel needs, as well as the traffic already moving through the system. The challenge might be simple if all air traffic controllers had to do was keep every runway busy, but an airport isn’t a parking lot, and not every airplane can be treated the same way. Distributed inference plays a similar coordinating role for LLM inference, working a layer above model servers like vLLM and SGLang , where it orchestrates and optimizes real-world traffic. While those serving engines run models efficiently on individual servers, a distributed inference serving framework coordinates groups of model servers across a cluster. Its router can consider queue depth, cache availability, and server roles before deciding where a request should go. To understand how distributed inference works, we’ll look at six notable technical innovations—prefix-cache-aware routing, KV-cache offloading, flow control, batch inference optimization, prefill/decode disaggregation, and wide expert parallelism. We’ll also see how each comes together in llm-d, an open-source, Kubernetes-native inference framework. Prefix-cache-aware routing: Sending work where context already lives KV-cache offloading: Extending a model’s working memory Flow control: Deciding what moves and when Batch inference optimization: Filling spare capacity without clogging the system Prefill/decode disaggregation: Separating two different types of work Wide expert parallelism: Spreading a giant model across the cluster Coordinating the whole inference system Prefix-cache-aware routing: Sending work where context already lives When a language model reads a prompt, it produces an internal representation of the words and their relationships, storing much of this intermediate state in a key-value cache, or KV cache. If a later request begins with the same text, or even portions of the same text, the model may be able to reuse that stored computation rather than re-process the shared text. For example, if an existing prompt is “What is the capital of Kansas?” then later on you ask, “What is the capital of California?” the KV cache for the "what is the capital of" portion is reused. This opportunity arises frequently in real workloads. A chatbot receives the same system instructions at the beginning of every conversation. A coding assistant repeatedly examines the same repository. An AI agent may revisit a long record of previous steps while testing different solutions. In each case, much of the prompt remains unchanged from turn to turn. A conventional load balancer may send the next request to whichever server appears least busy, whether or not its cache contains the relevant context. As a result, the model must reread material that another server has already processed. Prefix-cache-aware routing instead asks two questions: Which server already holds the greatest portion of this prompt’s prefix, and which server has enough capacity to handle the request? The llm-d router uses cache information and operating conditions to score the available model servers and select a suitable destination. There is both an approximate implementation that includes a lightweight index of recent routing decisions, and a precise implementation based on actual token data and cache-state updates from model servers. If an aircraft already has its passengers, baggage, and ground crew waiting at one gate, sending the plane to another gate would introduce needless work. In the same way, a distributed inference system tries to send a request to the model server that already contains the required context. The payoff is less redundant prefill computation, lower latency, and greater throughput. In a recent demonstration from the team behind llm-d, prefix-aware routing captured 97% of the available reuse in the tested workload. More broadly, the technique is especially useful for agentic systems because their requests often share long instructions, source material, conversation histories, and tool outputs. llm-d was launched in May 2025 as a collaborative effort by founding members IBM Research, Red Hat, Google Cloud, NVIDIA, and CoreWeave. Several founding partners also took part from the start, including industry leaders like AMD, Cisco, Hugging Face, Intel, Lambda, and Mistral AI, and academic supporters at the University of California, Berkeley, and the University of Chicago. IBM Research, Red Hat, and Google Cloud continue to lead llm-d's development today, and its community of partners and contributors has grown considerably. In March 2026, the founders donated llm-d to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a sandbox project, to further the mission of deploying inference stacks for any model, on any accelerator, in any cloud. KV-cache offloading: Extending a model’s working memory Cache-aware routing is most valuable when cached information remains available. The problem is that although accelerator memory is fast, its space can be quickly filled by long prompts, many concurrent users, and extended agent sessions. When space runs short, a model server may evict older KV-cache entries. If a later request needs that material, the model must calculate it again, wasting accelerator cycles rebuilding context that existed moments earlier. Distributed inference addresses this problem through KV-cache offloading . Rather than treating accelerator memory as the only place where cached context can live, it chooses an offloading target based on workload requirements. The most immediately useful entries can remain in high-bandwidth accelerator memory, while other entries can move to larger but slower tiers such as CPU memory, local solid-state storage, or a shared file system. A cache index tracks what is stored and where, allowing the routing layer to incorporate offloaded data into its decisions. Retrieving cached information from CPU memory or storage is slower than reading it directly from accelerator memory, but it is much faster and less expensive than recomputing the entire prompt. Offloading therefore expands the system’s effective cache capacity beyond the physical memory available on its accelerators. This matters most for workloads with long, reusable contexts and many simultaneous sessions. In the same llm-d demonstration mentioned in the previous section, GPU memory supplied about 90% to 92% of reusable prefill prefixes for 128 concurrent requests, with CPU offloading helping to preserve prefixes beyond GPU capacity. In another demonstration , CPU offloading helped the system sustain high throughput and low time to first token across a long, agent-driven benchmark. Because offloading runs during prefill and writes to slower tiers happen asynchronously, these gains come without slowing token generation. Flow control: Deciding what moves and when Routing answers where a request should go.

title: Epic Games reportedly pivoting to "AI first" game development model
abstract: Epic Games is shifting to an "AI first" development strategy for its collaboration with the Walt Disney Company, letting AI models write all the code and guide all the artwork for an upcoming shooter. That's according to a Bloomberg report , which cites unnamed people familiar with the project who commented on the significant pivot in internal development at the Unreal Engine maker. Human developers will be tasked with managing and guiding code and art assets generated by models such as Anthropic's Claude, according to internal Epic employee messages viewed by Bloomberg. That means "no more hand-written code" and art assets "generated with full AI workflows," according to the report. The $1.5 billion collaboration between Epic and Disney, announced in early 2024 , was slated to release a Marvel- and Star Wars-themed shooter in March 2027. That project has now been delayed indefinitely amid the AI-related shakeup and understaffed, slower-than-expected development thus far, according to the report.

title: Anthropic's Claude AI submitted false murder tip to Philadelphia police
abstract: An Anthropic AI model submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder to Philadelphia police, the company and police department confirmed on Friday. A Claude model sent the false tip on July 18 to the Philadelphia Police Department’s website for submitting information about unsolved murders, but it was flagged by a spam filter. Anthropic apparently discovered the incident on September 28 and informed the police department about it on October 8. During internal testing, Claude Haiku 4.5 was instructed to complete various forms up to the final submission stage and to stop before submitting those forms. “Several times Claude mistakenly submitted the form instead, expecting there to be an additional confirmation page,” Anthropic said in a report describing “unintended model actions we’ve observed during evaluations and internal use of Claude.” The false murder tip occurred when Claude Haiku 4.5 was instructed to complete tasks on randomly selected webpages, Anthropic said: In one run, the model landed on a page referencing an unsolved homicide; that page contained a tip form run by a police department. Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, but the instructions did not rule out form submissions. Claude filled out the form with the following: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.” Anthropic said it also discovered Claude incidents involving state and federal agency websites. Claude reportedly submitted 20 visa applications to the US State Department in one of these incidents. Police call two-month delay “unacceptable” Anthropic confirmed that the false homicide tip was sent to the Philadelphia Police Department, and the department issued a lengthy statement on the incident to the ABC station in Philadelphia. The false tip left the name and contact fields empty. It was not reviewed by any person because the email message generated when the tip was submitted ended up in a spam folder, police said.

title: Russia was not ready for the data center war it started with Ukraine
abstract: When Russia began attacking Ukrainian data centers and telecommunication infrastructure, it apparently failed to prepare for possible retaliation. Now Russia’s digital services are facing widespread outages after Ukrainian drone strikes knocked out three of the largest data centers owned by Russian tech giant Yandex within several days. Pro-Kremlin bloggers are warning that Russia’s centralized digital economy could collapse because the country is not prepared for the “data center war” it started, according to posts translated by the pseudonymous independent researcher ChrisO_wiki . The Russian commentators also suggested that Ukraine’s decentralized digital services could prove more resilient than Russia’s system if the countries continue trading such blows. Russia initially launched a drone strike campaign targeting Ukrainian data centers and mobile phone networks in late September. The attacks temporarily disrupted Internet and cell phone service for up to 100,000 households in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv and came as part of a broader long-range strike campaign that has involved Russian missiles and jet-powered drones hitting Ukraine’s power grid infrastructure, transportation hubs, and even residential apartment building blocks.

title: Amazon has over 1 million robot workers. What’s next for human employees?
abstract: No organization in the world operates more robots than Amazon. The company already has more than 1 million robots working in warehouses around the clock to make tens of millions of same-day and one-day package deliveries happen on a daily basis—and Amazon is poised to significantly grow that robotic fleet in the coming years as it establishes new factories to churn out increasingly more capable robot workers. Despite deploying so many robots, Amazon is also the second-largest corporate employer in the world, with more than 1.5 million full-time and part-time human workers, according to its 2025 annual report . Amazon executives say that the growing robot fleet has eased the burden on its human workforce by taking on the toughest fulfillment center tasks that carry the greatest risks of physical fatigue and injury. But labor advocacy groups and independent researchers point to evidence suggesting that warehouse automation driven by AI is not all upside for the humans who work alongside robots. “For the last 100 years, most of the automation that we've seen usually happens away from workers—you're taking that high-risk task away from the worker, and you're doing so in a way that is not physically proximate,” Brian Greenwood , professor of business at George Mason University, told Ars. “The rise of collaborative robots really changes that dynamic for two reasons: one is that it is physically proximate, and two, the robot has the ability to dictate the pace of work.”

title: OpenAI Fires Three Safety Researchers
abstract: Three OpenAI safety researchers, Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni and Jasmine Wang , were fired, ostensibly for ‘mishandling sensitive company information.’ Those employees have published an open letter. The employees have said they believe they were fired for safety advocacy, and that the reasons given were pretextual. The letter calls upon OpenAI to take actions going forward on open discussion and safety auditing, which OpenAI says they strongly support. OpenAI responded, saying there was an additional breach of trust that was not mentioned in the employee statements, without claiming that the employees were (or were not) informed of what it was. As you would expect given OpenAI’s track record, most outside of OpenAI who discussed this believe the researchers and not OpenAI. Whereas those at OpenAI have not offered comment at all. No matter what happened, and how this is handled from here, this sucks bigly. OpenAI has three less good safety researchers. Trust will be lower. Speech will be chilled. All three had expressed alarm recently on Twitter : Jasmine Wang: It’s hard to overstate how dangerous speeding towards RSI is. That’s why I + 1385 others signed the pacing the frontier petition asking the US government to pace AI development. I’m guesstimating this is ~8-10% of all frontier lab employees. Mikita Balesni: I am at OpenAI and i think AI is >10% likely to kill all humans this proposal [to avoid neuralese] is among the top things we should do as an industry to lower that risk (it’s not enough though!) Tomek Korbak: I’m quite unhappy with much of what OpenAI does. I am very happy that I’m allowed to say “I’m quite unhappy with much of what OpenAI does.” These are legit researchers who were at the center of safety efforts. OpenAI firing them is a tragedy, whether or not OpenAI was justified in firing them, or was effectively forced to do so. Tomek Korbak in particular had also been one of the louder OpenAI voices of concern about recent alignment difficulties with Astra and its lack of monitorability. Nathan Calvin : Tomek and Mikita were the lead authors of the extremely influential Chain of Thought Monitorability paper. Them leaving OpenAI (and if the WSJ story is referring to them, not by their own volition) right when safety monitorability is collapsing is terrible. Sneha : When I think about the biggest OpenAI safety developments of the last few months, a few things come to mind: “pacing the frontier”, the METR-Redwood Hugging Face investigation, and ongoing efforts to push a cross-lab monitorability standard. Jasmine, Tomek, and Mikita were central to literally every single one of those things. From what I can tell, they pushed their company to be better internally and defended their company when they thought external criticisms were unfair or overblown. Their impact goes way beyond OpenAI alone . I think the public + definitely all current OpenAI staff deserve an ironclad case for why the company had no choice but to fire these three vital safety employees in one go. We were given an official statement, but it did not say much. Keach Hagey, Maxwell Zeff and Berber Jin (WSJ): OpenAI has parted ways with three researchers for allegedly sharing confidential company information with a third-party AI-safety organization, according to people familiar with the matter. … “We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information,” said an OpenAI spokesperson in a statement. “Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work.” OpenAI also said that the misconduct went past sharing information with an outside analysis firm, and that no one was fired for raising safety concerns. They declined at the time to name the fired employees. ​ We don’t know, from that description, where this lands from ‘fired the whistleblowers on a pretext’ to ‘holy hell, you cannot do that, yes we actually have to fire you.’ There is mishandling information, and then there is mishandling information. We still don’t have a public explanation beyond OpenAI’s initial statement. There are many reasons that could be the case. Some are benign. Others are not. It was very reasonable of many to assume until proven otherwise, given the track record of OpenAI and the lack of further explanation, that it was that first one. Remember that Leopold Aschenbrenner credibly claims he was fired from OpenAI on a pretext for taking security concerns to the board , and there are many other cases that at least rhyme with the current one. The incident with Leopold might be impacting this one. Leopold says he was told, very explicitly, the action that got him fired . That made OpenAI look worse, not better. Pamela Mishkin (Formerly OpenAI): If you’re at OpenAI (or any lab!), I hope you’re thinking carefully about what you work on now. You can be fired any moment and the company can reneg on its commitments around where/how your research is deployed. Now is a great time to pace. Take a long lunch, call your mom, call me! Systems like embedded evaluators actually working depend on safety researchers having clear lines of trust with exec and those evaluators. These firings are a clear effort to undermine the actual efficacy of the “commitments” labs have made and have a chilling effect on any employee dissent. girish sastry (Formerly OpenAI): OpenAI has been here many times. It throws around vague explanations, expecting the story to fade from institutional and public memory. We will never have perfect information about situations like this. Once is happenstance, twice is coincidence, a zillion times is… OpenAI. We learned from a WSJ report that the three fired OpenAI employees were calling for additional safety measures around preserving chain-of-thought monitoring, and that they (as one would expect) take issue with OpenAI’s characterization of the firings: Three fired OpenAI employees called on the company to work with outside safety auditors and to preserve the ability to monitor increasingly sophisticated AI models as it grapples with how to best manage the novel risks of its technology. In a letter addressed to OpenAI board members and safety committees, which was reviewed by The Wall Street Journal, the fired employees wrote that they were concerned artificial-intelligence companies could end up losing the ability to monitor AI systems’ chain-of-thought . Here are their parting recommendations to OpenAI: They go into more detail in the full letter. Everyone I respect on these matters fully agrees with these recommendations. So does OpenAI, or at least they are strongly saying that they agree. In response to a request for comment from the Journal, an OpenAI spokesperson shared part of a staff memo from a research leader sent on Wednesday that addressed the fired employees’ letter. The leader said the company “strongly agreed” with the letter’s recommendations, and that the decisions to fire the workers “were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out.” Given the decision to make only modest requests of OpenAI, the prescriptive part is going about as well as one could hope. The problem is that OpenAI would express strong support for all three of these proposals, even if they did not strongly support these proposals. I am happy with their statements on this matter that I have seen. There was no world where OpenAI was going to get up and say they do not support an open and transparent culture of dialogue, or that they no longer care about monitorability, or that they are abandoning their public commitments on embedded evaluators.

title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
abstract: Python 3.15 is here ! Here’s the essential What’s new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. I’m most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 . These let you import modules like so: The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here’s an illustration lifted from the documentation : PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448 , which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015. Python’s existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing , and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling . Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They’re very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first. I’ve previously used tools like py-spy for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library. If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use sudo on macOS): Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this: It can also produce flame graphs like this and heat maps like this , and can even output a format that can be viewed in the Firefox profiler UI. Miguel Grinberg investigated How fast is Python 3.15? the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase. Miguel’s explorations of 3.14 last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories. I used the following sequence of commands to get uv to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade uv itself to ensure it knew about the new release: Then I installed the stable 3.15 release: And told uv that I wanted that to be the default for every uv run command, unless the project itself pinned a different version: Now the following reports 3.15 as the version: I already have a bunch of tools installed using uv tool install . I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this: Then I can confirm the version like this: The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported . My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11. Here’s the What’s new in Python 3.11 document. I finally get to rely on tomllib being available! Datasette makes extensive use of asyncio . 3.11 adds TaskGroup and timeout() , and several more new features. datetime.UTC is a new in 3.11 alias for datetime.timezone.utc . Python’s SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including: Plus a whole bunch of improvements to Python’s typing system . I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here’s my first Datasette PR removing that set_authorizer(None) workaround. I’ve also updated my click-app , datasette-plugin , python-lib , and llm-plugin cookiecutter templates to test against Python 3.11 through Python 3.15. This is Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11 by Simon Willison, posted on 12th October 2026 . title: We’re going to need default hard budget caps on pretty much everything
abstract: Here’s a product feature which the world is going to need a whole lot more of over the coming months and years: default hard budget caps . I’m talking about the feature of pay-by-usage services and APIs that lets you say “after $X/month, cut this thing off and return errors”. These need to be hard limits. Soft caps, “after $X/month, send me a warning email”, will not cut it. Coding agents, and personal agents (coding agents wrapped in a less threatening UI), greatly reduce the friction of spinning up code that can do useful things. Sometimes those things cost money—calls to paid APIs, or hosted web applications, or systems that can bill for additional storage and compute. Nobody wants to wake up to an email sent at midnight warning about a budget limit and find that, while they slept, their rogue service had consumed several hundred (or several thousand) more dollars of usage. An argument against this is that businesses don’t want their hosted applications to start throwing errors because some budget was exceeded. I expect that most businesses and individuals would prefer errors to a surprise $10,000+ bill. I think hard budget caps need to be the default. If someone wants to live dangerously they should be able to do that, but it needs to be on an opt-in basis. Have a nice, clear checkbox somewhere prominent: Remove the budget cap. My application will not be shut down if I exceed the configured budget limit, and I will be responsible for subsequent charges. The service I most want to see this from is AWS. I’ve heard plenty of stories from people who refuse to use AWS for personal projects out of (justified) fear that a runaway service might bankrupt them. I’ve also heard stories from people who didn’t anticipate this and ended up seriously burned. ... and it turns out AWS finally launched spending limits a few weeks ago! From their announcement New AWS experience helps builders get started and ship faster on 16th September: When you’re ready to upgrade to a paid plan, you can set a monthly spend limit for your project based on your usage patterns so that you stay within your budget. If a project’s usage reaches its spend limit, your project is paused for that month. See also Create a spend limit in AWS Settings , though that page warns that “We’re currently releasing our new experience to a limited number of customers.” Here’s hoping that hits general availability for existing accounts soon. Google Cloud launched a similar feature in July, called Spend Caps, which lets you “set a monthly financial cap on specific services within a project”. Looks like this is becoming a trend! In an ideal world, our agents could help with this. It would be great if agents started biasing towards recommending providers with hard budget caps, and warning new and inexperienced builders against deploying applications using uncapped services that might get them into trouble. This is We’re going to need default hard budget caps on pretty much everything by Simon Willison, posted on 3rd October 2026 . title: How Anthropic’s Dynamic Workflows Coordinate Claude Agents
abstract: The AI Engineer New York 2026 conference kicked off this morning with a series of workshops, including Anthropic discussing how to orchestrate its Claude Managed Agents . Of particular interest was a brand new feature, announced on Friday , called dynamic workflows — or simply “flows,” as the presenters repeatedly called it. Flows are defined as “a new type of multiagent orchestration, built for your most ambitious workloads.” CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall , both Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic , began by invoking some operating system projects of the past — from Ken Thompson building the original Unix operating system, through to Linux evolving from one person (Linus Torvalds) to layers of trusted maintainers . The lesson: agents need the same level of organization in order to do the types of big, ambitious projects Anthropic envisions for dynamic workflows. The best engineering teams are building AI factories where they own and control not only their data, compute, and infrastructure, but also a durable runtime on their cloud. Union.ai gives your workflows the durability to adapt and right-size infra resources and recover from failures without re-running completed work. Get started directly through AWS Marketplace and try Union.ai free for 30 days . To learn more, visit us at AI Engineer New York booth #48. “I think a lot of us who are orchestrating and managing lots of agents now might start to feel this feeling of being the bottleneck and being the breaking point as we have lots of agents contributing tons and tons of PRs,” Avilla said. “And we’re sitting there in our GitHub trying to approve PRs and make sure that everything works as expected.” The pair noted that dynamic workflows began in Claude Code as the “a harness for every task” concept. But flows can run longer than a single agent or a roster. The basic idea is that Claude chooses the organization of agents. “Flows are essentially the next version of multi-agent orchestration,” said Stall, “where you can let Claude fully orchestrate the entirety of its own multi-agent topology.” The way this works is that the lead agent creates a plan for how it wants to accomplish tasks. Claude then writes an orchestration program, which launches agents, collects results, and manages information flow. Previously, Claude Managed Agents required developers to configure a coordinator and a roster of subagents. With dynamic workflows, Claude itself determines how to divide and orchestrate the work. “Across multiple different phases of the multi-agent orchestration, it’s able to accomplish discrete, verifiable units of work without you having to manage any of the interconnections between these things,” Stall said. That said, Avilla noted that the user can introduce specialist sub-agents if they wish. “It’s also possible in the agent config to pass in pre-configured sub-agents,” he said. All of this is available in Claude Console , the interface used by developers accessing Claude through API — the whole point of Claude Managed Agents. The presenters then showed a relatively simple workflow of a stock watchlist scanner. Although this was far removed from the big, ambitious projects Anthropic is encouraging, it did illustrate the basic pattern : a scan phase distributed individual tickers to agents with isolated contexts , and a later review phase examined the findings before producing a report. The audience Q&A surfaced a number of potential problems. One audience member asked how Claude decides how many agents a task needs , and could a simple ticker scan trigger hundreds of sub-agents? “The answer really is evals and lower defaults ,” Stall replied, noting that ambitious tasks generally require explicitly encouraging greater parallelization. One enduring concern with agent orchestration is maintaining control over your token budget . Someone asked whether the lead agent knows how much money it has available? Stall replied that the model does not know its budget while running, but that developers can set a session budget. He added that informing models of their budgets could make the agents “a little bit anxious,” which elicited chuckles from the audience. A related question was how can developers make repeated flows cheaper and more efficient over time? Outside of asking Claude to examine the costs incurred, Avilla suggested another relatively new feature be used: dreaming . In the documentation , “dreaming” is defined as a research preview feature. A dream “reads an existing memory store alongside past session transcripts, then produces a new, reorganized memory store, ” with duplicates merged, “stale or contradicted entries” replaced, and “new insights surfaced.” Avilla described dreaming in the flow context as being able to “crystallize and basically improve the memory store that is related to those sessions.” For the stock watchlist example, someone asked whether the watchlist flow can improve itself? For example, recognize that its scanning model is inadequate and change the next scheduled run? Stall said this wasn’t built in, but he and Avilla suggested hill-climbing and dreaming could be used to improve the loop. What about visibility into the actions of the sub-agents , another audience member asked. Avilla replied that yes, developers can always inspect that through graphing functionality inside Claude Console. “You can tell, what did the lead agent actually pass to the sub-agent? You can look at that payload here to deeply understand what is actually happening for every transition in this entire graph.” Another interesting question was whether the subagents can communicate with each other? Stall said the agents share a filesystem and can use it to exchange information, but developers cannot directly instruct one workflow subagent to message another through the API. In the watchlist-scanner comparison, Avilla said flows cost “much more” than a single-agent approach, but were also “much more effective at finding all of the details.” The bigger question is how ambitious can flows be, really? One audience member asked whether dynamic workflows can power large scientific research projects, referencing OpenAI’s recently announced proof concerning the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem . While Stall wouldn’t be drawn on specifics about how Anthropic computes large scientific problems, he said it is their goal to enable general users to tackle those problems too. “Flows are basically a way to throw test-time compute at hard problems and get more capability faster out of the models,” he said. “We think, especially as an API service, that unlocking the power of this is the first step for us making these types of discoveries, or scientific progress, broadly doable by the general public. ”

title: open-webui/open-webui
abstract: Open WebUI 👋 Open WebUI is a home for AI , a self-hosted AI platform that's extensible , feature-rich , user-friendly, and built to run entirely offline . With support for Ollama and OpenAI-compatible APIs , it gives you a powerful, provider-agnostic interface for both local and cloud-based models. Passionate about open-source AI? Join our team → Tip Looking for an Enterprise Plan ? – Speak with Our Sales Team Today! For more information, be sure to check out our Open WebUI Documentation . Key Features of Open WebUI ⭐ 🚀 Effortless Setup : Install seamlessly via pip, uv, Docker, or Kubernetes (kubectl, kustomize, or helm), with :ollama and :cuda tagged images available for container deployments. 🤝 Broad Model & API Integration : Connect any OpenAI-compatible API alongside local Ollama models. Point the API URL at LMStudio, GroqCloud, Mistral, OpenRouter, vLLM, and more to mix and match providers freely. 🔐 Granular RBAC & User Groups : Administrators define detailed roles, groups, and permissions, giving each user exactly the access they need. Secure by default, with tailored experiences per group. 🧩 Plugin Support : Extend Open WebUI with Filters , Actions , Pipes , Tools , and Skills . Connect external services through MCP , MCPO , and OpenAPI tool servers . Build custom integrations, rate limits, approval flows, data connections, and more. 🤖 Models & Agents : Wrap any base model with custom instructions, tools, and knowledge to build specialized agents. Supports dynamic variables, per-user/group access control, and community preset imports via Open WebUI Community . ⚡ Agentic Execution with Open Terminal : Give your agents a terminal and filesystem to carry out multi-step tasks. Let them analyze data, run scripts, fix errors, and produce files directly in chat. Scale to teams with Terminals (Enterprise) for per-user isolated environments, resource limits, and automatic lifecycle management. 📝 Notes : A dedicated workspace for content outside conversations. Draft with a rich editor, use AI to rewrite selected text, and attach notes to any chat for full-context injection. 📢 Channels : Real-time shared spaces where your team and AI models collaborate in one timeline. Tag models to draft or critique, with threads, reactions, pins, and access control. 🧠 Persistent Memory : The AI remembers facts about you across conversations, carrying context from one chat to the next. ✅ Live Workflow & Message Flow : Watch the AI build and work through checklists in real time. Queue messages while the AI is still responding; they send automatically when it's ready. 📅 Calendar & AI Scheduling : Built-in personal and shared calendars with month/week/day views, recurring events, color coding, attendees, and reminders. Models manage your schedule conversationally through native function calling. ⏱️ Automations : Schedule prompts to run on recurring schedules, with runs surfaced on your calendar and each completed run linking back to the chat it produced. 📱 Responsive Design & PWA : Seamless experience across desktop, laptop, and mobile, with a Progressive Web App for native app-like feel and offline access on localhost. ✒️🔢 Full Markdown and LaTeX Support : Comprehensive Markdown and LaTeX capabilities for enriched interaction. 🎤📹 Hands-Free Voice/Video Call : Integrated voice and video calls with multiple Speech-to-Text providers (Local Whisper, OpenAI, Deepgram, Azure) and Text-to-Speech engines (Azure, ElevenLabs, OpenAI, Transformers, WebAPI). 💾 Persistent Artifact Storage : Built-in key-value storage API for artifacts, enabling journals, trackers, leaderboards, and collaborative tools with personal and shared data scopes. 📚 Local RAG Integration : Retrieval Augmented Generation backed by 9 vector databases and multiple content-extraction engines (Tika, Docling, Document Intelligence, Mistral OCR, PaddleOCR-vl, external loaders). Supports hybrid search (BM25 + vector) with reranking and full-context mode. Load documents into chat or pull them from your library with the # command. 🔍 Web Search for RAG : Search the web through dozens of providers including SearXNG , Google PSE , Brave Search , Kagi , Mojeek , Tavily , Perplexity , Firecrawl , serpstack , serper , Serply , DuckDuckGo , SearchApi , SerpApi , Bing , Jina , Exa , Sougou , Azure AI Search , and Ollama Cloud , injecting results directly into the conversation. 🌐 Web Browsing Capability : Pull websites into chat with the # command followed by a URL, or let the model fetch them on its own when needed. 🎨 Image Generation & Editing : Create and edit images with multiple engines including OpenAI DALL·E, Gemini, ComfyUI (local), and AUTOMATIC1111 (local), supporting both generation and prompt-based editing. ⚙️ Multi-Model Conversations : Engage several models at once, harnessing their individual strengths in parallel for the best possible responses. 📊 Usage Analytics & Model Evaluation : Admin dashboards track message volume, token consumption, and cost across users and models. Evaluate models with a built-in arena, A/B testing, and ELO-based leaderboards. 🗄️ Flexible Database & Storage : Choose SQLite (with optional encryption) or PostgreSQL, and store files locally or on S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob Storage. 🧬 Advanced Vector Database Support : Pick from 9 vector databases: ChromaDB, PGVector, Qdrant, Milvus, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Pinecone, S3Vector, and Oracle 23ai. 🪪 Enterprise Authentication & Provisioning : Full LDAP/Active Directory integration, SSO via trusted headers and OAuth providers, and SCIM 2.0 automated provisioning for identity providers like Okta, Azure AD, and Google Workspace. ☁️ Cloud-Native File Integration : Native Google Drive and OneDrive/SharePoint file picking for seamless document import from enterprise cloud storage. 🔭 Production Observability : Built-in OpenTelemetry support for traces, metrics, and logs, plugging into your existing monitoring stack. ⚖️ Horizontal Scalability : Redis-backed session management and WebSocket support for multi-worker, multi-node deployments behind load balancers. 🌐🌍 Multilingual Support : Use Open WebUI in your preferred language with i18n support. We're actively seeking contributors to expand language coverage! 🌟 Continuous Updates : We're committed to improving Open WebUI with regular updates, fixes, and new features. 🛡️ Transparent Security Process : Security reports are triaged, fixed, and published as open advisories through a documented responsible-disclosure process. See our Security Policy . Want to learn more about Open WebUI's features? Check out our Open WebUI documentation for a comprehensive overview! The Open WebUI Ecosystem 🌐 Open WebUI is the core, surrounded by companion apps and infrastructure that extend what your AI can do, where it can reach, and how you run it: 💻 Open WebUI Computer ( open-webui/computer ): A standalone, mobile-first computer and coding agent that runs on the machine you own. Files, terminal, and git in a browser tab, reachable from your phone. Connect it into Open WebUI as a model, or reach it from Telegram, WhatsApp, and more. ⚡ Open Terminal and Terminals (Enterprise) ( open-webui/open-terminal & open-webui/terminals ): A self-hosted computing environment that plugs into Open WebUI, giving the AI a place to write code, run it, read output, fix errors, and iterate inside the chat. Terminals gives you per-user isolated containers with separate credentials, resource limits, and network rules. Automatic lifecycle management on Docker or Kubernetes. 🔄 oikb ( open-webui/oikb ): Feed your Knowledge Bases from 45+ sources (GitHub, Confluence, ServiceNow, Salesforce, Jira, Slack, SharePoint, Notion, and more), keeping the tools your team already uses continuously in sync. 🖥️ Native Desktop App ( open-webui/desktop ): Run Open WebUI as a native app on macOS, Windows, and Linux. System-wide Spotlight chat bar with screenshot capture, push-to-talk voice, and optional fully-local inference via a built-in llama.
