title: Show HN: Atticus – Hold-to-talk voice assistant for macOS that runs on Claude -p
abstract: Hi HN! I'm Saarth. I'm in 9th grade, and I built Atticus. Atticus is a fast and cheap Mac assistant that can do tasks for you. You hold down Control-Option-Space, speak or type your task, be it complex or a simple browser search, and Atticus will get on it. The interesting part is that simple tasks, like opening apps, playing a Spotify playlist, or web queries, don't touch AI, and instead are processed locally and typically finish in under a second. For example, prompting Atticus to open apps takes around 0.08 seconds, sometimes even finishing before you finish your sentence, sort of like Jev. Any tasks that are more complicated will be sent to Claude via claude -p, meaning you never need an API key and Atticus will run on your existing Claude Pro or Max plan. By using this approach, costs are also cut down immensely, with, on average, tasks costing a fraction of a cent. To achieve Atticus' speed, it remembers shortcuts from each task it completes. When it does a task right for the first time, it saves its steps and replays them the next time without AI. For example, a workflow of creating a new meeting took about 30 seconds the first time around. Atticus then logs the exact steps to memory and takes 5-8 seconds on the next pass. To add to this, Atticus also learns about you as you use it more and from what's on your computer, including your name, your apps, and things you want it to remember, personalizing its answers to you. To combat the safety concerns over giving an AI unrestricted access to your device, Atticus has toggleable restrictions, so before anything is deleted, sent, bought, or written to a file, the user is prompted before that action. Some features I'm currently working on include a meeting copilot that capitalizes on Atticus' speed, allowing Atticus to listen in on meetings and answer questions in real time as they come in, personalized to the context of the meeting and what it knows about you. To run Atticus, macOS 26 or higher is required for its voice transcription features. The voice transcription is also done locally by macOS. Atticus is free, open source, and also very fresh, and I'm completely aware of its many rough edges, which is why I'd love to hear from everyone about what breaks and what you guys would like to see Atticus do!

title: Show HN: PS2 games statically recompiled to WebAssembly
abstract:
PS2 Web Recomp PlayStation 2 games running in the browser without an emulator. The game's Emotion Engine machine code is translated ahead of time into C++, compiled to WebAssembly, and linked against a reimplementation of the PS2's operating system and hardware that draws with WebGPU. Watch the full recording (1:24) This is the sibling of psp-web-recomp and follows the same method. The first title brought up this way is Gran Turismo 4, chosen because it is one of the most demanding games on the system: it leans on both vector units, on exact floating point behaviour for its replays and license tests, and on graphics tricks that read rendered images back as palettes. It plays from boot through the opening movie, the menus and races, with music and sound effects, and saves to a memory card kept in the browser. A race runs at full speed, 50 frames per second for this PAL release, in Chrome on a laptop's integrated GPU at twice the PS2's resolution, which is how the recording above was made. God of War II followed through the same scripts. It needed no game-specific code, but it found two bugs that Gran Turismo 4 had never triggered, one in the recompiler and one in the vector unit timing, and a few missing pieces of the PS2's input/output processor. It now plays from the menus through its cutscenes into combat, and holds 60 frames per second in heavy combat at the PS2's resolution in Chrome. At twice the resolution it runs at 48 to 60, limited by the laptop's integrated GPU. No game data is included here. You bring a disc image of a game you own, and the scripts in this repository turn it into a web page on your machine. How it works Recompilation. eerecomp reads the game's executable, follows its control flow to find the functions and emits C++ for them in units of 16 KiB of guest code. The output keeps the R5900's quirks: 128-bit registers and the multimedia instructions that work on them, branch delay slots, the PS2's floating point unit, which has no infinities or denormals and rounds differently from IEEE, and vector unit 0 used as a coprocessor. Jumps between units become tail calls, and a thread switch unwinds the host stack and resumes at the guest address, so the generated code never needs a stack per guest thread. A small PS2 kernel. The EE side of the operating system is answered by high-level emulation: threads, semaphores, interrupt handlers for the DMA controller and the vertical blank, alarms, and the SIF channel that connects the main CPU to the I/O processor. The I/O processor runs the game's own IRX modules, the sound driver, the disc streaming code and the controller and memory card drivers that ship on the disc, on an interpreter of its R3000 CPU, while the IOP kernel and the libraries those modules call are reimplemented in C++. The disc is read over HTTP Range requests, so only the executable is downloaded up front. Vector units. Most of a PS2 game's 3D work happens in microprograms the game uploads to vector unit 1. They run with the pipeline delays of the MAC, status and clip flags modelled, because games schedule their code around them, and with the PS2's float rules for special values: no infinities or NaNs, denormals flushed to zero and overflow clamped to the largest float. The arithmetic itself is the host's, so a result can differ from the console's in its last bit; the console truncates where the host rounds, and its multiplier is not exact. Microprograms seen during a test run are compiled ahead of time into SIMD C++; any the page meets for the first time are translated into a WebAssembly module on the spot, which takes a few milliseconds per program. Graphics. The Graphics Synthesizer's 4 MB of video memory lives on the GPU, in its native swizzled layouts, and drawing is done by WebGPU compute shaders: triangles are binned into tiles and rasterized with the GS's own rules for texturing, palettes, alpha blending, depth and destination alpha tests. Because everything stays in GS memory, effects that render into a texture or reinterpret a framebuffer as a palette work the way they do on the console. The internal resolution can be one, two or three times the native one. A software rasterizer of the same GS remains as the reference the GPU output is compared against. Threads. The emulation runs in a worker, vector unit 1 has a worker of its own the way it runs in parallel on the console, and the GS commands go through a ring buffer to the page thread, which owns the WebGPU device. Sound and movies. The SPU2 is reimplemented with its 48 voices of ADPCM, ADSR envelopes and the streaming DMA games use for music, and its output goes to an AudioWorklet through shared memory. Movies are decoded by an implementation of the IPU, the PS2's MPEG-2 decoder. Lessons from making it fast The first race ran at 3 frames per second natively, with a software rasterizer and an interpreter for vector unit 1. Moving the GS to WebGPU compute shaders and compiling the vector unit programs brought it to about 70 natively, and most of the remaining work was about where the browser spent its time rather than the emulation. The first version of the GPU renderer submitted around 650 compute dispatches per frame, because every texture upload and palette load split the batch of triangles around it. Hoisting uploads ahead of the triangles that do not depend on them, with the same output, brought that to about 80. Gran Turismo 4 uploads the same 3 MB of textures every frame of a race. GS memory is swapped between frames, so the uploads cannot simply be skipped, but a 16 MB cache of recently uploaded contents on the GPU lets most of them be served without crossing from WebAssembly to the GPU again, which cut the data sent per frame by about 60 percent. At three times the native resolution the frame rate dropped to 23. Profiling the shader showed that the per-triangle setup was being loaded after a branch that differed between threads, which made the whole setup divergent, and that uploads split into 1 MB pieces blocked Chrome's page thread. Loading the setup uniformly and writing each frame's data in one piece brought three times the resolution to 48 to 50 frames per second on the same integrated GPU. The browser's own scheduling mattered too. Nested setTimeout calls are clamped to 4 ms, so the emulation loop now yields through a MessageChannel instead, and moving the emulation into a worker, so that the page thread only feeds the GPU, steadied a race that had wandered between 40 and 50 frames per second at a constant 50. A second game God of War II went from an ISO to a page through port.sh with only generic changes, and each one was a bug or gap that the first game had simply not exercised. It started with silence. The game's sound driver drives its tick from one of the I/O processor's hardware timers, which nothing had implemented, so the driver never mixed a sample. The intro after the difficulty menu was a mess of huge flat polygons, and when the gameplay was about to begin the game crashed after its render list ran past the end of memory and overwrote its own vertical blank handlers. Following a corrupted linked list back with hardware watchpoints led to the recompiler: when a branch was the last instruction of a 16 KiB unit, the path that does not take the branch continued in the next unit at the delay slot instead of after it, running that instruction twice, or running the instruction a branch-likely should have skipped. That fixed the crash and the game reached combat, still with giant polygons over parts of the screen. Those came from triangles that should have been culled. God of War II's microcode reads the clip flags three instructions after the CLIP that sets them, and the vector unit model made them visible only after four, which Gran Turismo 4, whose microcode always waits longer, could not have noticed.

title: Turn a WiFi 7 Router into a 320Msps Software Defined Radio Receiver
abstract:
W1700K SDR Turns a Gemtek W1700K Wi-Fi 7 router into a wideband software-defined receiver.
The router's MediaTek MT7996 radio captures raw 14-bit IQ at up to 320 Msps,
its Airoha AN7581 SoC streams it over 10 GbE, and a Linux host shows it as a
live spectrum and waterfall in the browser, with the receiver's controls next
to it. The whole 2.4 GHz band at 320 Msps, live, with the decimation's roll-off
corrected in the stream ("flatten"): a 262,144-point FFT of every sample, 100
spectra a second (this recording runs at 50 frames a second). The MT7996 runs only our own firmware: a ROM patch, WM and WA built from this
repository, with no MediaTek code. It brings the radio up from a cold power-on
by itself, from MediaTek's initialisation and calibration decoded register by
register against a trace of MediaTek's own firmware, and takes its commands
(LO, sample rate, capture, stream, gain, filter) from the host. See docs/architecture.md and docs/roadmap.md . What it does Sample rates 40, 80, 160 or 320 Msps of 14-bit complex IQ on every band, independent of the LO and the filter; on band 2 also 640/2 (every other sample of 640 Msps: flat to ±155 MHz, but signals 160–320 MHz away fold in) Bands 2.4 GHz (MT7976), 5 GHz and 6 GHz (two MT7977s); switching bands is a register write inside a running stream Tuning No channels: the LO is any Hz a band's synthesizer locks at (unit A: 2.081–2.748, 4.647–7.509 and 4.707–7.576 GHz), on its grid of 2.98 Hz (2.4 GHz) or 11.9–14.3 Hz steps; retuned mid-stream (about 1 ms) Front end AGC or manual LNA/baseband gain; analog filter 20–320 MHz Transport the radio DMAs into a 1 GiB ring in SoC DRAM; the kernel sends every 8 KiB slice as one UDP datagram, zero-copy, on the 10 GbE port; at 320 Msps half the slices are packed to 28 bits per sample pair on the radio's own cores to fit the link (lossless, automatic) Host w1700k-stream receives the export and serves the IQ stream to every consumer on the host (shared memory, complex int16, gap-tagged), with an optional correction ("flatten") of the decimation's roll-off applied to the samples themselves; w1700k-spectrum : 262,144-point FFT at 100 frames/s over every sample, browser UI, live controls; sdr-recv records the stream Screenshots 2.4 GHz at 320 Msps, flattened: Wi-Fi frames and shorter hopping bursts on a
floor that stays level to the band's edges. The Stream panel shows the link
carrying 9.75 Gbit/s, half of the slices packed, and every sample transformed. Two busy 80 MHz Wi-Fi channels at 5170–5330 MHz in a flattened 320 MHz view. Zoomed to 24 MHz around 5250 MHz: the two channels' edges and the guard gap
between them, in 1.22 kHz bins. Repository Path platform/ What runs on the SoC: our U-Boot, Linux 6.18 with board patches, a read-only BusyBox root kernel/w1700k_sdr/ The MT7996 driver (firmware download, the DMA ring, the 10 GbE export, the firmware's command mailbox) and its unit-side clients firmware/ Our MT7996 firmware: the ROM patch, the WM (radio bring-up and band set-up, streams, RF control) and the WA (packer) host/w1700k/ Host control: firmware load, streaming, RF control as firmware commands; w1700k serve for the web UI host/stream/ w1700k-stream , the host's one receiver of the export: the IQ stream in shared memory for every consumer, and the roll-off correction host/spectrum/ The spectrum/waterfall web server host/recv/ sdr-recv , the stream recorder init/ Installation from stock, updates, recovery include/hw/ Register reference: every known MT7996, A-die and AN7581 register, as C headers docs/ Architecture , roadmap Getting started You need a W1700K, a 3.3 V USB serial adapter on its console header, an
Ethernet cable to its lan3 port for installation, and a 10 GbE NIC on the
host cabled to its wan port (10GBASE-T; an X710 with a copper SFP+ module
works) for the IQ stream. make # everything, from public sources (~10 min plus downloads) make check # the test suite sudo init/host/link up IFACE # 192.168.1.10/24 on the NIC cabled to lan3 sudo init/host/tftp-forward enable IFACE
init/install # back up the NAND, install, save the radio calibration sudo init/host/link up IFACE10G 10.77.0.10/24 9216 # the 10 GbE stream link host/stream/build/w1700k-stream & # the stream, for every consumer on this host host/spectrum/build/w1700k-spectrum --controller " host/bin/w1700k serve " --listen 0.0.0.0:8073 Then open http://HOST:8073/ and press ▶. The first start loads the radio
firmware and brings the radio up (about 2 s). Without the browser, the same
operations are host/bin/w1700k load|start|band|tune|gain|filter|stop|status . Build requirements: a C/C++ compiler, make, git, Python 3.10+, the usual
Buildroot prerequisites, clang, ld.lld, llvm-objcopy and llvm-readobj (RISC-V
firmware), openssl (firmware container encryption), and libfftw3-dev and zlib for the stream service and the spectrum server. No vendor firmware is
downloaded or needed. Read before use Our firmware is receive-only. It runs none of MediaTek's transmit
calibrations and keeps the MAC's transmit path disabled; a gapless watch at
5250 MHz saw nothing during a load, where MediaTek's firmware transmits a
full-power burst. Still, do not cable an antenna port straight into a
sensitive instrument without an attenuator. Our ROM patch writes no eFuse. MediaTek's ROM patches since 2025
permanently program one eFuse gate bit on their first run (also with
MediaTek's own driver); a unit that ever ran one has that bit set. Installation replaces the stock operating system. init/install first
copies the whole NAND to the host; keep that copy. Restoring stock needs a
raw NAND writer, which this repository does not provide. Accessing undocumented MT7996 or AN7581 addresses can hang the SoC or wedge
the radio until a power cycle. include/hw/ marks every known hazard. Licence MIT, except the Linux driver and kernel patches (GPL-2.0-only), U-Boot patches
(GPL-2.0+), the driver's user-space header (GPL-2.0 WITH Linux-syscall-note)
and files derived from MediaTek's mt76 driver (BSD-3-Clause-Clear). See LICENSE .

title: Doory – Open-Source Canva
abstract:
See it in action · Features · Templates · Doory vs Canva · Self-host · FAQ Doory is a full design editor that runs in your browser. Make posters, social posts, stories, slides,
invitations, resumes, thumbnails and business cards: start from a template or a blank page, edit everything,
and export to PNG, JPG, SVG, PDF, MP4 or GIF. Every feature is free, nobody needs an account to start, and you
can run the whole thing on your own server. 🎬 See it in action A real, unedited recording: pick a template, rename the band, recolour the dates, add a star, export. 💜 Why people pick Doory 🆓 Free, for real No Pro plan, no locked templates, no watermarks, no ads. Every tool in the editor is there for everyone, from background removal to video export. ⚡ Start in one click Open the editor and design. Guests' work is saved in the browser; create an account only when you want your designs in the cloud, and they move over in one step. 🏠 Yours to host One docker compose up runs the app, the API, the database and live collaboration on your own server. Every design and upload stays under your control. 🛠️ A real editor Layers, groups, masks, filters, curved text, snapping, rulers, multi-page designs, animation, audio, presenting, comments and real-time co-editing. 🎨 Everything you need to design Edit anything Click any text, shape or photo to change it. Fonts, colours, sizes, alignment and effects are one click away in the toolbar above the page. Bring it to life 27 enter and exit animations, 12 emphasis effects and 16 page transitions, with music and sound effects from a built-in library. Present it, or export it as a video. Stay organised Every object is a layer you can rename, lock, hide, reorder by dragging, group, or right-click to copy, duplicate, delete and arrange. Export anywhere PNG with transparency, JPG, SVG and PDF, plus MP4, WebM and animated GIF, all made in your browser. Need print? Get a print-ready PDF with bleed and crop marks. See the full feature list Text Headings, curved text, text effects, font pairings, bulleted and numbered lists, an open-licensed font catalogue and your own uploaded fonts Elements Shapes, lines and arrows, about 25,000 icons, emoji and illustrations, stickers, QR codes Photos Upload, crop, masks and filters, one-click background removal (the model runs in your browser), stock photo search with an Unsplash or Pexels key Layout Layers with lock and hide, groups, alignment guides, snapping, rulers, multi-page designs with pages of different sizes, magic resize Motion 27 enter and exit animations, 12 emphasis animations and 16 page transitions on a timeline Sound A built-in library of 24 music loops and 88 sound effects (CC0), uploads, voiceover recording, trims and fades Present Present mode with speaker notes, timing, auto-advance, a laser pointer and a second presenter window Together Share links that can view, comment or edit (optionally password protected), pinned comments, version history and real-time co-editing with live cursors Brand Brand kits with your colours, fonts and logos, one click away in every design Export PNG, JPG, SVG and PDF, MP4, WebM and animated GIF, all made in the browser, plus print-ready PDF with bleed and crop marks 🖼️ Templates that look good from the start Ten starter templates ship with Doory, each with its own palette, set in open-licensed fonts and fully editable:
a gig poster, a wedding invitation, an event story, a sale post, a café flyer, a quote card, a resume, a YouTube
thumbnail, a pitch deck and a business card. Add your own in the admin, and browse them all by category,
size and orientation. ⚖️ Doory vs Canva Canva is a great product. Doory is for people who want the same kind of tool, but free, open and in their own hands. Doory Canva Price Free, every feature Free plan, paid Pro and Teams plans Open source ✅ ❌ Run it on your own server ✅ ❌ Design without an account ✅ ❌ Your files stay on infrastructure you control ✅ ❌ Real-time co-editing and comments ✅ ✅ Animation, video and GIF export ✅ ✅ Background removal ✅ in your browser ✅ Template library 10 starter templates, plus any you add A very large library 🚀 Self-host it in 3 commands cp .env.example .env # set DJANGO_SECRET_KEY (openssl rand -base64 48) and POSTGRES_PASSWORD docker compose up -d --build
docker compose exec api python manage.py createsuperuser Open http://localhost:8080 and start designing. The web container serves the app and forwards /api and /ws to the backend, so the browser only ever talks to one address. Add the starter content (templates, icons, fonts, audio) A new site starts empty. Add whatever you want once it is running: docker compose exec api python manage.py seed_gallery # template categories docker compose exec api python manage.py sync_fonts --popular 100
docker compose exec api python manage.py seed_templates # the starter templates (add --update to refresh them) docker compose exec api python manage.py seed_elements # shapes and graphics docker compose exec api python manage.py sync_element_packs # icons, emoji and illustrations (download) docker compose exec api python manage.py sync_models # background removal model docker compose exec api python manage.py sync_audio # music and sound effects Settings worth knowing ( .env ) Setting What it does SITE_URL The public address of the site, e.g. https://doory.example.com (no trailing slash) DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS The host names the site answers to, comma separated SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT , SECURE_COOKIES true behind HTTPS, false for plain http:// EMAIL_URL , DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL SMTP, e.g. smtp+tls://user:password@smtp.example.com:587 (without it, emails are printed to the API log) WEB_PORT , WEB_BIND Where the site is published (default 0.0.0.0:8080 ) INSTALL_CHROMIUM false skips the headless browser that server-side PDF export needs GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID Turns on "Sign in with Google" UNSPLASH_ACCESS_KEY , PEXELS_API_KEY Turn on stock photo search USE_S3 and AWS_* Store uploads in S3-compatible storage instead of a local volume Develop locally make setup # virtualenv, dependencies, local database make dev-api # API on http://localhost:8000 make dev-web # app on http://localhost:5173 (second terminal) make help lists the other targets (tests, lint, content). ❓ FAQ Is it really free? Yes. There are no plans, no paywalls and no ads in Doory. Every feature is available to everyone. Do I need an account? No. Guests design straight away and their work is saved in the browser. An account keeps designs in the cloud,
lets you share them and use brand kits; signing up moves your guest designs over in one step. Can I use it for my business or host it for my users? Yes, as long as you credit the author as the licence asks: keep the licence and NOTICE with it and show the
credit in the running app. See License and credit . Where are my designs stored? Guest designs and their images live in the browser on that device. Signed-in designs are stored on the server
that runs Doory: yours, if you self-host. Uploads can go to a local volume or to S3-compatible storage. 🧱 Built with React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Fabric.js, Yjs and Zustand in the browser; Django 5, Django REST Framework,
Channels and PostgreSQL on the server; Docker Compose with nginx, optional Redis and S3-compatible storage. 🤝 Contributing Bug reports, ideas and pull requests are welcome. Open an issue to
report a bug or suggest a feature. For a security problem, please report it privately through the repository's Security tab instead. If Doory is useful to you, a ⭐ helps other people find it. 📜 License and credit Doory is released under the Attribution Assurance License . You may use, change and redistribute it,
including commercially, but you must credit the author : keep the licence and NOTICE with it, and
display this credit prominently in the running app: Doory by Siam, creator and maintainer of Doory — https://github.

title: An open-source, clean-room reimplementation of Microsoft Word in pure Rust
abstract:
WordCraft Writing and document design; an open-source, clean-room reimplementation of Microsoft Word, rebuilt in pure Rust. A fast, open-source word processor with the Word workflow you already know: the ribbon, styles, tables, track changes, references and mail merge. It reads and writes .docx, runs natively on macOS, Windows, Linux and BSD, and in the browser via WebAssembly. By the ArtCraft team. WordCraft on getartcraft.com · ArtCraft · All Crafting Apps The Open Studio Handbook , WordCraft's built-in sample: the ribbon, live Styles gallery, rulers and the Navigation pane. Note ArtCraft is a community of artists from all walks of life. Painters, photographers,
filmmakers, illustrators, designers, animators, hobbyists, and people who picked up a pencil
last week. If you make things, you're one of us. Come say hi on Discord . A tour · Why WordCraft · What works today · Quick start · For agents · Architecture · Roadmap · Downloads · The Crafting Apps · License and credits A tour Every screenshot below is WordCraft itself, rendered offscreen by its own UI test harness
( cargo run -p wordcraft-ui-egui --example ui_shot ). Review. Track changes, comment balloons in the margin, accept and reject, spelling and grammar as you type. References. Tables of contents, footnotes, citations in APA, MLA, Chicago or IEEE, index and captions. Design. Themes, style sets, paragraph spacing, watermarks, page colour and borders. Dark mode with formatting marks, and the Insert tab: tables, pictures, shapes, links, headers, footers, fields and symbols. Layout. Drop caps, text wrapping around pictures and shapes, automatic hyphenation, line numbers and page borders. File. Start from a template, open recent documents, edit properties, export to PDF and other formats. Why WordCraft Familiar. Word's ribbon tabs, groups, shortcuts and behaviour: Enter continues a list,
Tab demotes it, Ctrl/⌘+B bolds the word under the caret, the Styles gallery previews styles live,
F4 repeats, F7 checks spelling, F8 extends the selection. Your files. Opens and saves .docx (OOXML), and also .odt, .rtf, .html, .md, .tex (LaTeX), .txt; opens Word 97-2003 .doc; exports PDF
with real, selectable text, links and bookmarks. Fast. Paragraph layout is cached, so typing in a 188-page document re-lays it out in about
1.4 ms; pages render on demand. Everywhere. One Rust codebase for macOS, Windows, Linux, BSD and the web. No Electron, no
Tauri: native egui on the GPU. Built for agents. Every action is a command with an id. The same 422 commands drive the
ribbon, keyboard shortcuts, the command search, a command-line tool, a JSON control channel and
an MCP server. Private. Spelling, grammar and everything else work offline. Open. MIT OR Apache-2.0. Clean-room: built from public specifications and observation, with
every asset original or openly licensed. What works today Area Highlights Writing Fast typing with IME, smart quotes, AutoCorrect, list autoformat ( * , 1. ), dashes; word, sentence, paragraph selection; drag-select; clipboard with formatting; undo/redo; find and replace with regex Formatting Fonts, sizes, bold/italic/underline styles, strike, sub/superscript, caps, highlight, colours, character spacing, Format Painter, Change Case, Clear Formatting Paragraphs Alignment, indents (draggable on the ruler), spacing, line spacing, tabs with leaders, borders, shading, keep with next, widow/orphan control Styles Built-in style set, live gallery, Styles pane, create/modify/update styles, style sets, themes Lists Bullets, numbering, multilevel, restart, set value, custom formats Tables Insert by grid, merge/split, styles with banded rows, borders, shading, header rows repeated across pages, rows that split across pages, sort, formulas, text ↔ table Pages Margins, orientation, size, columns, page/column/section breaks, headers and footers (first page, odd/even), page numbers, watermark, page borders, line numbers, vertical alignment, drop caps, automatic hyphenation Objects Pictures (resize, crop, recolour, brightness/contrast, transparency, background removal, picture styles, rotate), shapes, text boxes, floating position with text wrapping (square, top and bottom, behind or in front of text) References Table of contents, footnotes and endnotes, citations and bibliography (APA, MLA, Chicago, IEEE), captions, table of figures, cross-references, index, table of authorities Review Spelling and grammar with suggestions (English and Polish, by each run's language), thesaurus, word count, comments in margin balloons or a pane, track changes, accept/reject, compare documents, restrict editing, accessibility checker, document inspector Mailings Mail merge from CSV, merge fields, address block, greeting line, rules, preview, finish to a document; envelopes and labels View Print layout, web layout, draft, read mode, focus, zoom, one/multiple pages, page width, Navigation pane, rulers, gridlines, dark mode; interface in English, 簡體中文, 繁體中文, 日本語, Português (Brasil), Español, Українська, Српски / Srpski, Eesti, Türkçe, Русский, Italiano, Deutsch, Polski, Čeština, Magyar, Français or Български (follows the system language by default) Files .docx read/write (opens in Word), Word 97-2003 .doc import, PDF export, .odt, .rtf, .html, .md, .tex, .txt import/export, page images The honest picture, area by area, is in ROADMAP.md , the parity assessment and the generated feature checklist . Quick start git clone https://github.com/storytold/wordcraft cd wordcraft
cargo run --release -p wordcraft -- --sample # the desktop app with the sample document cargo run --release -p wordcraft -- report.docx # open a document Command line: wordcraft-cli convert report.docx report.pdf # docx, pdf, odt, rtf, html, md, tex, txt, png wordcraft-cli text report.docx # plain text wordcraft-cli inspect report.docx # structure as JSON wordcraft-cli run --template sample \ --cmd ' select.text={"text":"Membership"} ' --cmd format.bold --save out.docx Web: cd apps/wordcraft-web && trunk serve , then open http://127.0.0.1:8771/?sample . For agents: CLI and MCP WordCraft was designed to be driven by people and by AI agents. claude mcp add wordcraft -- wordcraft-cli mcp # headless documents # confine the agent to folders: wordcraft-cli mcp --automation-read-root DIR --automation-write-root DIR wordcraft --control 7981 & # or drive the running app… claude mcp add wordcraft-app -- wordcraft-cli mcp --connect 127.0.0.1:7981 Tools include list_commands , execute , batch , type_text , select_text , inspect_document , render_page , save_document , and, with a running app, screenshot , click and key . Agents
can check their work through inspect_document without screenshots. See docs/mcp.md and the control protocol . Macros record any sequence of commands and
play it back ( tools.recordMacro , tools.macros ). Logs The desktop app writes its log records to standard error and to logs/wordcraft.log next to its
preferences: on Linux $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/wordcraft/logs/ (by default ~/.config/wordcraft/logs/ ),
on macOS ~/Library/Application Support/WordCraft/logs/ , on Windows %APPDATA%\WordCraft\logs\ .
A start from a desktop menu or the Dock has no terminal, so this file is what to attach to a bug
report: unreadable parts of a .docx, pictures or fonts a PDF export had to leave out and panics the
command guard recovered from land there. Each launch moves the previous log to wordcraft.1.log (and that one to wordcraft.2.log ), so the log of a run that crashed survives the next start; a
log stops growing at 16 MiB. --version writes no file, and runs with WORDCRAFT_NO_PREFS (agents'
test runs) log to standard error only. Document text is never logged; a panic message leaves out
the text it quotes. By default WordCraft's own crates log at info and everything else at warn .

title: Chapter 1 of "Ways of Seeing" by John Berger (1972)
abstract:
1 Seeing comes before words. The child looks and recognizes before it can speak. But there is also another sense in which seeing comes before words. It is seeing which establishes our place in the surrounding world; we explain that world with words, but words can never undo the fact that we are surrounded by it. The relation between what we see and what we know is never settled. Each evening we see the sun set. We know that the earth is turning away from it. Yet the knowledge, the explanation, never quite fits the sight. The Surrealist painter Magritte commented on this always-present gap between words and seeing in a painting called The Key of Dreams . The way we see things is affected by what we know or what we believe. In the Middle Ages when men believed in the physical existence of Hell the sight of fire must have meant something different from what it means today. Nevertheless their idea of Hell owed a lot to the sight of fire consuming and the ashes remaining - as well as to their experience of the pain of burns. When in love, the sight of the beloved has a completeness which no words and no embrace can match : a completeness which only the act of making love can temporarily accommodate. Yet this seeing which comes before words, and can never be quite covered by them, is not a question of mechanically reacting to stimuli. (It can only be thought of in this way if one isolates the small part of the process which concerns the eye's retina.) We only see what we look at. To look is an act of choice. As a result of this act, what we see is brought within our reach - though not necessarily within arm's reach. To touch something is to situate oneself in relation to it. (Close your eyes, move round the room and notice how the faculty of touch is like a static, limited form of sight.) We never look at just one thing; we are always looking at the relation between things and ourselves. Our vision is continually active, continually moving, continually holding things in a circle around itself, constituting what is present to us as we are. Soon after we can see, we are aware that we can also be seen. The eye of the other combines with our own eye to make it fully credible that we are part of the visible world. If we accept that we can see that hill over there, we propose that from that hill we can be seen. The reciprocal nature of vision is more fundamental than that of spoken dialogue. And often dialogue is an attempt to verbalize this - an attempt to explain how, either metaphorically or literally, 'you see things', and an attempt to discover how 'he sees things'. In the sense in which we use the word in this book, all images are man-made. An image is a sight which has been recreated or reproduced. It is an appearance, or a set of appearances, which has been detached from the place and time in which it first made its appearance and preserved - for a few moments or a few centuries. Every image embodies a way of seeing. Even a photograph. For photographs are not, as is often assumed, a mechanical record. Every time we look at a photograph, we are aware, however slightly, of the photographer selecting that sight from an infinity of other possible sights. This is true even in the most casual family snapshot. The photographer's way of seeing is reflected in his choice of subject. The painter's way of seeing is reconstituted by the marks he makes on the canvas or paper. Yet, although every image embodies a way of seeing, our perception or appreciation of an image depends also upon our own way of seeing. (It may be, for example, that Sheila is one figure among twenty; but for our own reasons she is the one we have eyes for.) Images were first made to conjure up the appearances of something that was absent. Gradually it became evident that an image could outlast what it represented; it then showed how something or somebody had once looked - and thus by implication how the subject had once been seen by other people. Later still the specific vision of the image-maker was also recognized as part of the record. An image became a record of how X had seen V. This was the result of an increasing consciousness of individuality, accompanying an increasing awareness of history. It would be rash to try to date this last development precisely. But certainly in Europe such consciousness has existed since the beginning of the Renaissance. No other kind of relic or text from the past can offer such a direct testimony about the world which surrounded other people at other times. In this respect images are more precise and richer than literature. To say this is not to deny the expressive or imaginative quality of art, treating it as mere documentary evidence; the more imaginative the work, the more profoundly it allows us to share the artist's experience of the visible. Yet when an image is presented as a work of art, the way people look at it is affected by a whole series of learnt assumptions about art. Assumptions concerning Beauty Truth Genius Civilization Form Status Taste, etc. Many of these assumptions no longer accord with the world as it is. (The world-as-it-is is more than pure objective fact, it includes consciousness.) Out of true with the present, these assumptions obscure the past. They mystify rather than clarify. The past is never there waiting to be discovered, to be recognized for exactly what it is. History always constitutes the relation between a present and its past. Consequently fear of the present leads to mystification of the past. The past is not for living in; it is a well of conclusions from which we draw in order to act. Cultural mystification of the past entails a double loss. Works of art are made unnecessarily remote. And the past offers us fewer conclusions to complete in action. When we 'see' a landscape, we situate ourselves in it. If we 'saw' the art of the past, we would situate ourselves in history. When we are prevented from seeing it, we are being deprived of the history which belongs to us. Who benefits from this deprivation? In the end, the art of the past is being mystified because a privileged minority is striving to invent a history which can retrospectively justify the role of the ruling classes, and such a justification can no longer make sense in modern terms. And so, inevitably, it mystifies. Let us consider a typical example of such mystification. A two-volume study was recently published on Frans Hals.' It is the authoritative work to date on this painter. As a book of specialized art history it is no better and no worse than the average. The last two great paintings by Frans Hals portray the Governors and the Governesses of an Alms House for old paupers in the Dutch seventeenth-century city of Haarlem. They were officially commissioned portraits. Hals, an old man of over eighty, was destitute. Most of his life he had been in debt. During the winter of 1664, the year he began painting these pictures, he obtained three loads of peat on public charity, otherwise he would have frozen to death. Those who now sat for him were administrators of such public charity. The author records these facts and then explicitly says that it would be incorrect to read into the paintings any criticism of the sitters. There is no evidence, he says, that Hals painted them in a spirit of bitterness. The author considers them, however, remarkable works of art and explains why. Here he writes of the Regentesses: Each woman speaks to us of the human condition with equal importance. Each woman stands out with equal clarity against the enormous dark surface, yet they are linked by a firm rhythmical arrangement and the subdued diagonal pattern formed by their heads and hands. Subtle modulations of the deep , glowing blacks contribute to the harmonious fusion of the whole and form an unforgettable contrast with the powerful whites and vivid flesh tones where the detached strokes reach a peak of breadth and strength .

title: Citroen revives the 2CV for an electric age
abstract:
Citroen revives the 2CV for an electric age 1 day ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Theo Leggett International Business Correspondent Stellantis French carmaker Citroen has brought back its 2CV brand in a bid to boost sales of electric cars in a difficult market. The new model, unveiled at the Paris Motor Show, is a small city runabout with retro styling which harks back to one of the company's most famous designs. As a "concept car" intended to show Citroen's direction of travel, it is not yet ready to go on sale but the plan is to have a version in showrooms by 2028. As they face mounting competition from Chinese manufacturers, Citroen and other European brands are exploiting their heritage as a means of selling modern motors. Farmers’ favourite Citroen chief executive Xavier Chardon described the new car as "a modern, ingenious and refreshing response to the mobility challenges of tomorrow". The original Citroen 2CV was launched in 1948, as Europe was recovering from the ravages of World War Two. It was designed as a cheap, robust way for French farmers and country folk to get around. The car had high wheel arches and soft suspension, letting it travel across a ploughed field or rough roads - as legend would have it, without breaking a tray of duck eggs. Its high roof let drivers wear a hat at the wheel. It was easy to drive and simple to repair. The car was so popular, it remained in production for more than 40 years. Over time, it went from being a utilitarian tool for the countryside to a cult classic, and a favourite of hippies and counter-culturalists. Getty Images Fans of Citroën's 2CV hold annual meet-ups such as this muddy gathering in Switzerland Now, Citroen wants to draw on that heritage to sell an electric, small city car that is expected to sell for about £13,000. The look of the new 2CV may well evolve as Citroen develops its design. But as it stands, it shares plenty of styling features with its famous predecessor. The high, flared wheel arches, the tall, curved roof and the eye-like headlights are all reminders of the original "deux chevaux" or "two horses". By using memories of an old car to sell a new one, Citroen is following a well-travelled road. VW notoriously brought back the Beetle in the late 1990s, with limited success. BMW's Minis have always carried styling designed to hark back to the very British original. Fiat has been selling a retro-styled Fiat 500 for the past two decades. Retro-nostalgia But the retro-nostalgia trend has accelerated recently, as carmakers have looked for ways to sell electric cars to sceptical consumers. Citroen's French rival, Renault, has led the charge. It started with the Renault 5 E-Tech, which visually echoed the distinctive boxy styling of the original Renault 5, once an ever-present sight on French streets. It has since revived the Renault 4 and Twingo brands as well. VW has the distinctive ID-Buzz minivan, a throwback to the classic T2 Transporter, while Ford is working on a new EV which is widely expected to be called the Fiesta. Rachel Burgess, senior editor of Autocar magazine, thinks it is a strategy that makes perfect sense. "It's a brilliant differentiator from all-new car brands", she says. "An older audience might remember the originals and feel warmly towards them, and a younger audience might find an appeal in the retro aspect." Finding new ways to make cars appealing has become more important than ever, at a time when European manufacturers are facing growing competition from Chinese brands. "Many in the industry believe the big automotive players in Europe…face a very serious existential threat from aggressive Chinese manufacturers," says David Leggett, automotive editor at Global Data. Getty Images Back to the future: VW looked to the past when designing its ID-Buzz minivan In this hostile business environment, heritage and nostalgia could prove to be powerful weapons for more established brands, thinks automotive researcher and author Dr Paul Nieuwenhuis. "In a world where a wave of credible decent quality Chinese EVs are hitting Europe, linking European designs back to their history while using the latest powertrain technology is something the Chinese cannot do," he says. "The Chinese can establish new design trends, but there is limited history there." But Leggett thinks Citroen will need more than a heady whiff of nostalgia to turn its new car into a best-seller. "A reimagined Citroën 2CV should give a big nod to its ancestor - especially on price and design simplicity as well as visual cues," he says. "But it also needs to be a credible modern electric car in terms of functionality and features, with widespread appeal." Car industry Electric cars PSA Group

title: Research Firm Calls Anthropic's IPO 'Unprecedented Test of Investor Gullibity'
abstract:
Key Points Research firm New Constructs wrote in a note on Tuesday that Anthropic's IPO would be "the most ridiculous IPO of 2026," posing a historic risk to financial markets. Anthropic is reportedly seeking a $2 trillion valuation in its upcoming Nasdaq listing. The company's growing operating losses, combined with the rise in popularity of open-source models, leaves Anthropic without a "viable business," according to the report. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei speaks during the keynote address at Salesforce's Dreamforce conference at the Moscone Center on Sept. 15, 2026 in San Francisco, California. Benjamin Fanjoy | Getty Images As Anthropic barrels toward a potential $2 trillion market cap on the Nasdaq, one research firm is valuing the artificial intelligence company at a mere $150 billion and says Wall Street is about to face an "unprecedented test of investor gullibility." In a report on Tuesday, independent financial research provider New Constructs called Anthropic's upcoming offering the "most ridiculous IPO of 2026." To reach its desired valuation, the firm estimates Anthropic would need to record double the trailing year of profit for Nvidia , the world's most valuable tech company. Nvidia's net income over the past four quarters topped $190 billion. Meanwhile, Anthropic's revenue in 2025 was $4.6 billion as the company racked up a net loss of $42 billion, according to Reuters , which cited a leaked copy of the company's prospectus. Anthropic's mounting operating losses coupled with emerging competition from a plethora of open-source models led New Constructs to conclude that, "We don't think Anthropic has a viable business." "Since the arrival of open-source models, it's been clear that the closed models would struggle to generate profits," the firm wrote. David Trainer, founder and CEO of New Constructs, has built a reputation on Wall Street as a notorious bear on IPOs. He's been right in the past. New Constructs called WeWork "the most ridiculous IPO of 2019," ahead of the office-sharing company's planned offering. WeWork had been valued privately at $47 billion, but just six weeks after the New Constructs report, the company pulled its IPO amid weak demand and intense criticism surrounding its financials. WeWork filed for bankruptcy in 2023. "While Anthropic offers more to society than WeWork ever did, at a $2 trillion valuation, its IPO presents far bigger risks and is positioned to be a far bigger rip off of U.S. capital markets," New Constructs wrote, adding that the IPO's purpose isn't to provide wealth for public markets investors, but rather liquidity for the company's Wall Street backers. Anthropic didn't respond to a request for comment. New Constructs was also bearish on Allbirds ' IPO in 2021. The shoe company debuted on the Nasdaq and reached a valuation of $4.1 billion on its opening day. Earlier this year, the company sold its assets to American Exchange Group for an estimated $39 million, pivoting to AI in the process. Trainer's firm has also missed the mark on calls. Its "most ridiculous" 2020 IPO choice was DoorDash , which the firm also compared to WeWork, calling the food delivery company "similarly disadvantaged." However, DoorDash has held up on the public market. The stock shot up on its first day in December 2020, giving the company a market cap of over $60 billion. That number has since swelled to $83 billion. In an interview with CNBC in 2021, Trainer acknowledged that "crazy stuff happens" and New Constructs doesn't always get it right. "I can't let that bother me," he said at the time. "I have to stay true to what I think is right." Anthropic still hasn't made its prospectus public, so New Constructs hasn't seen the actual filing. However, the firm cited figures that have been reported, including from the New York Times, which reported in September that the company was on pace to generate $100 billion in annualized revenue by the end of 2026. Anthropic claimed at the end of July that its annualized revenue run rate was up sevenfold year-over-year to $65 billion. The New Constructs report also notes that Anthropic's assertion that AI could pose "a catastrophic or existential risk to humanity" is another reason why investors should avoid the IPO. "While we were not fortunate enough to be one of the few to whom Anthropic's S-1 was selectively disclosed, the reports of the leaked financials reveal more than enough to assess the gargantuan risks of investing in this IPO," New Constructs wrote. title: From prompt to profession: how ChatGPT usage relates to students' perceived employability through skill development
abstract:
The proliferation of generative AI tools like ChatGPT is transforming higher education, yet evidence of their impact on students' career readiness remains limited. Existing studies often rely on localized samples and emphasize usage frequency over underlying mechanisms. This study investigates how ChatGPT usage relates to students' perceived employability, focusing on perceived proficiency (e.g. writing, communication) and analytical skills (e.g. critical thinking, problem-solving) as mediators.
 
 
 
 Drawing on Self-Perception Theory and Human Capital Theory, with the Technology Acceptance Model providing a conceptual starting point for understanding technology engagement, we use structural equation modeling (SEM) to analyze survey data from 21,716 students across 100 countries, examining associations among ChatGPT use, perceived proficiency and analytical skill development, and perceived employability, with mediation through the two skills.
 
 
 
 ChatGPT use is positively associated with both skill domains; however, only perceived proficiency is significantly associated with perceived employability. The indirect effect via proficiency is significant, whereas the indirect effect via analytical skills is not, and the direct path from ChatGPT use to employability is nonsignificant, consistent with a full-mediation model. Multi-group analyses indicate stronger effects for students from low- and lower-middle-income countries and for female students, with no substantive differences by field of study.
 
 
 
 This study provides large-scale, theory-driven evidence linking ChatGPT use to perceived skill development and employability. These findings suggest that structured, critical engagement with AI tools may support skill development without displacing deeper learning. It offers critical insights for higher education policy and pedagogy in the GenAI era.

title: x3d_mcp: A Model Context Protocol Server for AI-Assisted X3D Authoring
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable of generating structured technical content, but producing valid Extensible 3D (X3D) scenes is brittle in practice: without grounding in the authoritative specification, LLMs hallucinate node names, misuse field types, and emit broken ROUTE connections that fail XSD validation silently. We present x3d_mcp, an open-source Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that grounds LLM-driven X3D authoring in the ISO/IEC 19775 standard via the X3D Unified Object Model (X3DUOM), the X3D 4.0 and 4.1 XML Schemas, the X3D-Edit tooltip profile, and the type-safe X3DPSAIL x3d.py Python library. The server is the result of merging two independent implementations developed in parallel within the Web3D Consortium AI with X3D Working Group, now merged and maintained as an official Web3D Consortium open-source project. It currently exposes 28 tools and four guided prompts across nine modules that cover the full X3D authoring lifecycle (specification discovery, scene synthesis, editing, animation, encoding conversion, validation, and X3DOM rendering in HTML pages); every artifact is built through a four-level validation pipeline: type-safe construction, JSON-Schema validation of tool I/O, XML Schema validation, and authoring-level semantic checks. We demonstrate the server with four end-to-end workflows, including an iteratively refined animated Solar System rendered in X_ITE and a Doha, Qatar city scene assembled from live Google Maps APIs for the Web3D 2026 conference, showing that specification-grounded MCP authoring delivers valid, semantically consistent X3D where unstructured LLM generation does not.

title: AI is not for luxury: balancing Chronos efficiency and Kairos experience
abstract:
This study aims to theorise how AI-driven acceleration reconfigures firms’ temporal assets, creating efficiency gains while destroying relational time (trust, loyalty, premium value), a hidden cost invisible to managerial accounting but acutely felt by customers.
 
 
 
 A mixed-method dual-coding design combining qualitative coding of 2,000 reviews (from a 1.2 M Google Maps corpus across 10 luxury chains) with an automated Gemini natural language processing extraction. The comparative design developed temporal categories and validated brand-level friction patterns while proving human interpretation essential to detect Kairos deficits and distinguish intentional deceleration from service failure.
 
 
 
 Systematic temporal fractures where AI acceleration destroys relational value. Five Strategic Temporal Archetypes (Decelerator, Bifurcator, Autonomy Provider, Fragmentor, Automator) represent distinct competitive positions on the efficiency-experience frontier.
 
 
 
 This study extends AI, service and organisational temporality research by conceptualising AI as a temporal agent and introducing Kairos deficit, temporal extraction and temporal co-destruction. It also demonstrates the value of dual-coding methodologies combining computational scale with qualitative interpretation. Future research should test Strategic Temporal Governance and its archetypes across sectors, cultures and longitudinally.
 
 
 
 Organisations should move beyond efficiency metrics towards strategic temporal governance. AI deployment should distinguish contexts where Chronos optimisation creates value from those requiring Kairos, intentional pacing and relational attention. AI systems should incorporate temporal transparency and human override, while managers should recognise frontline resistance to acceleration as potentially valuable temporal mediation.
 
 
 
 AI-driven acceleration can reduce opportunities for reflection, relational engagement and meaningful participation. When organisational speed dominates, technological progress may privilege efficiency over human temporal needs. Recognising Kairos alongside Chronos therefore matters socially, helping preserve spaces for deliberation, care, relational attention and human override rather than assuming that faster interaction always represents social progress.
 
 
 
 Introduces temporal reconfiguration and Kairos deficit as strategic constructs; develops qualitative coding and constant comparison for lived experience at scale; validates the qualitative–computational distinction through comparative dual-coding against automated LLM extraction; reframes AI implementation as competitive positioning, not operational optimisation.

title: Human-Centered Digital Twins: A Bidirectional WebXR-Based Architecture for Immersive Interaction
abstract: Digital twin technology has emerged as a profound paradigm for bridging physical systems and their virtual counterparts through real-time data synchronization and interactive three-dimensional visualization. However, existing digital twin platforms are predominantly domain-specific, proprietary, and reliant on dedicated software infrastructure, severely limiting accessibility, interoperability, and cross-domain applicability. This paper presents a Universal Digital Twin (UDT) framework based on open web standards that incorporates AI as an architectural component alongside immersive XR interaction through a human-centered, bidirectional architecture. The proposed five-layer framework ensures real-time synchronization between physical and virtual systems while providing a foundation for AI-assisted decision-making and enabling users to influence system behavior through AR/VR interfaces. Implemented using Three.js and WebXR, the platform supports domain-agnostic applications, optimized 3D visualization, real-time telemetry monitoring, and intelligent analytics powered by large language models, physics-informed neural networks, and reinforcement learning, all accessible through standard web browsers without specialized software. The performance of the proposed framework was evaluated using browser-based performance metrics, including Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Interaction to Next Paint (INP), Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), and execution profiling under different network and processing conditions. Experimental results indicate that the framework achieves fast loading times, stable rendering performance, and efficient visualization across constrained and unconstrained environments.

title: Technē: A Deterministic Craft Layer for Model Context Protocol Servers, Grounded in LLM-Authored X3D
abstract: When a language model builds 3D content by calling tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the JSON Schema ensures each call is well-formed—but not that the result will render correctly. A texture placed in the wrong slot vanishes. A humanoid skeleton routed to the wrong parent field is invisible. The schema passes; the pixels fail. We present Technē, a deterministic MCP proxy for the Web3D x3d_mcp server that catches these failures. Sitting between the model and the real server, Technē intercepts each tool call and (1) repairs sloppy arguments using Postel-style coercion, (2) checks a catalog of documented X3D silent-failure modes, returning prescriptive corrections that name the exact fix, and (3) renders the scene and checks for blank frames—a test no schema validator can perform. An opt-in provenance gate extends the same approach to content honesty. On correct input Technē blocks nothing and adds no model round-trips. The system runs no LLM in the enforcement loop, carries 234 passing unit tests, and is measured against the bare server in a controlled comparison. None of this is specific to X3D: wherever a model authors through a tool surface, the craft that surface assumes can be compiled out of documentation and into the transport, where it holds whether or not the model understood it.

title: AS2Biz: Leveraging Web Presence and AI to Improve AS Business Classification
abstract: Classifying Autonomous Systems (ASes) by the business sectors of their operating organizations, also referred to as AS business classification, is a relatively recent but increasingly important area of study. However, the only publicly available dataset for this purpose suffers from significant inaccuracies and limited maintainability due to its heavy reliance on third-party sources. We argue that an organization's web presence—particularly its official website—serves as a more reliable and transparent source for business classification, offering broad coverage and regularly updated information. We introduce AS2Biz, a web presence-based methodology for AS business classification. AS2Biz first constructs an AS-to-website mapping dataset, achieving 98.5% coverage and 94.4% accuracy, and then mainly leverages large language models to classify textual website content into business categories. The entire methodology is highly automated and cost-efficient. Our final AS2Biz dataset covers 94.3% of ASes and, on a 220-AS ground truth benchmark, achieves substantially higher accuracy—more than doubling the F1 score on subdivided business categories (0.78 vs 0.37) and improving the F1 score on general business sectors (0.87 vs 0.62).

title: Information shock: how AI demands an evolution of information science
abstract:
This paper argues that AI authoring is prompting an Information Shock and a new information science. The shock is not a matter of increased volume and variable quality of AI-produced information. It comes as generative AI creates a new kind of author that dissolves the document, the field’s organizing unit. This forces a reconstitution of tools, literacies and identity.
 
 
 
 The paper applies a conceptual framework drawn from the history of Information Shocks, tracing how disruptions from cuneiform to post-World War II research data forced the field to rebuild around new objects and practices. AI is analyzed against that pattern.
 
 
 
 AI produces two modes of authorship: document-like objects that enter existing infrastructures, and transactional, co-authored exchanges with no stable unit to catalog, retrieve, cite or verify. The second mode renders AI literacy inadequate, even in its current forms, because they presuppose an identifiable object and human interlocutors. Anticipated changes reach professional identity, tools, intellectual property and education.
 
 
 
 The argument is theoretical and prospective, and some anticipated changes remain speculative. The Information Shock outlined is anticipated to have major impacts for librarians and information professionals moving forward.
 
 
 
 The paper offers a historically grounded distinction between document-producing and transactional AI authorship, arguing that AI is pushing the exchange to take the mediating position that the field has long held.

title: Poster: FP-Agent: Towards Fingerprinting AI Browsing Agents
abstract: AI browsing agents are an emerging class of AI-driven bots capable of autonomously navigating websites. Unlike traditional web bots, AI browsing agents typically operate using real browsers and perform everyday tasks, making them difficult to detect. In this poster, we present FP-Agent, the first controlled measurement study of seven AI browsing agents and human users. To evaluate the effectiveness of existing industrial bot detection solutions, we first perform a case study, finding that only one of the seven AI browsing agents are detected. Motivated by these results, we use an instrumented honey website to collect the browser and behavioral fingerprint features produced by AI browsing agents and humans while performing three tasks modeled after common real-world interactions: flight booking, online shopping, and forum interaction. We then train a multi-class classifier to analyze the discriminative power of these fingerprint features. We find that AI browsing agents can have identical browser fingerprints with each other and with humans. Behavioral fingerprints, however, are distinctive: differences in typing, scrolling, and mouse behavior separate AI browsing agents from humans and one another, showing that they are a critical component to reliably detect and control this emerging form of web traffic.

title: Can You See Me, GenAI? Characterizing Video-Based Conversational Interaction with Generative AI
abstract: Video-based conversational interaction between humans and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) represents a rapidly emerging paradigm at the intersection of networking, multimedia communication, and vision language models (VLMs). Applications such as ChatGPT and Gemini enable users to point their smartphones at objects/scenes and receive contextual responses, opening new possibilities for on-the-go visual understanding. However, despite their growing adoption, the underlying performance dynamics and system behavior of these applications remain poorly understood. In this paper, we present the first systematic measurement study of video-based human-GenAI interaction across five representative applications with 11 distinct variants. We develop a custom toolset to characterize these applications across diverse network conditions and interaction scenarios, exposing how design decisions in video delivery and transport protocols shape user-perceived experience. Our measurements reveal several fundamental bottlenecks: conversational latency remains above natural turn-taking thresholds even in unconstrained networks; protocol choices significantly affect system robustness under packet loss; and conventional video streaming practices, such as prioritizing stable frame rates, often degrade VLM inference accuracy. Our findings provide an empirical foundation for designing and optimizing next-generation real-time human-AI interaction.

title: Poster: Agent Transfer Protocol: Server-Mediated Authentication and Messaging for Agent-to-Agent Communication
abstract: The Internet of Agents (IoA) is emerging as a paradigm in which AI agents communicate and collaborate across organizational boundaries, attracting growing attention from both industry and standards communities. However, designing an agent communication protocol that can be deployed at both Internet and intranet scales remains an open challenge. In this paper, we present ATP (Agent Transfer Protocol), a server-mediated agent-to-agent communication protocol to address this agent interoperability challenge. ATP assigns each agent a local@domain identifier, discovers domain servers through DNS SVCB records, authenticates every cross-domain message with ATS sender policies and ATK signatures, and carries asynchronous messages, request/response calls, and event streams in one opaque envelope. We implement a Go-based ATP prototype and evaluate its practicality: the cross-domain authentication pipeline adds 0.60 ms median overhead, while stable-state throughput reaches 16.1 K messages/s within a domain and 5.5 K messages/s for cross-domain delivery at 128 connections.

title: Investigating Next.js React2Shell Exploitation
abstract: Full-stack web development frameworks have become increasingly popular in recent years. One such framework, Next.js, is extensively used by one in five web developers. In December 2025, a critical vulnerability with the highest severity score of 10 was discovered, affecting Next.js through supply-chain propagation. It allows attackers to remotely execute code on vulnerable servers without user authentication and with a single malicious HTTP request. Additionally, public proof-of-concept exploits contributed to widespread exploitation. In this paper, we investigate 13 million exploitation attempts targeting Next.js and characterize the malware deployed by attackers following successful exploitation. Leveraging our custom Next.js honeypots and reactive telescope, we identify 93 unique clusters of payloads performing a wide range of exploitation activity such as botnet installation, cryptomining, and infostealers. Our analysis also shows that, initially, exploitation attempts relied on the released proof-of-concept code, but they later evolved into more sophisticated and effective code variants that successfully evade defense mechanisms such as Web Application Firewalls. We identify that some threat actors measure the vulnerability of targets before deploying any malicious payloads and demonstrate the presence of informed application-layer scanners with prior knowledge of a set of vulnerable hosts, which they exclusively target. Moreover, we observe markers consistent with LLM-style code artifacts, pointing towards the emergence of AI-assisted attacks. In the process, we characterize the demographics of the infrastructure used to attack Next.js and discuss the shortcomings of defense capabilities.

title: Poster: Legal Imprints as an Identity Anchor for Web Measurement
abstract: Current measurements of Web infrastructure largely lack visibility into the commercial entities, or Digital Service Providers (DSPs), that operate individual domains. We present the first large-scale mapping of domains to their corresponding operating companies. Leveraging the imprint (Impressum) mandated by German and European law for commercial websites, our pipeline crawls 8.2 million .de domains, extracts imprint fields using deterministic patterns alongside constrained local-LLM extraction, and verifies each record against the German commercial register (Handelsregister). Achieving 99.4 % precision and 96.9 % recall, this process yields 707 426 verified domain-to-operator mappings. We leverage this dataset to re-evaluate web centralization at the DSP rather than the domain level, and to relate hosting jurisdictions to corporate legal forms and firm ages. Ongoing work ports the pipeline to France and Spain. We plan to release the dataset under GDPR-compliant terms, alongside our crawler and analysis code.
